### COS 221 — Computer Programming II

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cos-221
- 3 units · 200 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: undergraduates across University of Uyo programmes (foundation course, not departmental)

Advanced programming building on COS 211: deeper object-oriented programming (polymorphism, abstract classes, interfaces), the Collections API, searching/sorting/recursion, event-driven and GUI programming. Bridges programming skills and the algorithmic thinking required for security tool development.

**Outline**

1. Advanced OOP review: polymorphism, abstract classes, and interfaces
2. Class hierarchies and programme organization using packages/namespaces
3. Collections API: iterators/enumerators, List, Stack, Queue
4. Searching and sorting algorithms
5. Recursive algorithms
6. Event-driven programming: event-handling methods and event propagation
7. Exception handling
8. Graphical User Interface (GUI) programming

**Recommended textbooks**

- Data Structures and Algorithms in Java — Robert Lafore
- Introduction to Algorithms (CLRS) — Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein

**How to pass**

- VisuAlgo (visualgo.net) provides free visual animations for every data structure — use it constantly
- Implement every data structure from scratch at least once — never just read about it
- Trace sorting algorithms step by step on a 5-element array by hand before every exam
- Areté Java modules cover the programming foundation; use them for the Java component of this course

**Lecture notes** (12 transcribed topics; full text needs a free account)

1. Fundamentals in Java Programming
2. Flow Control Structures
3. Array
4. Methods (Functions)
5. OOP I: Concept of Object-Oriented Programming
6. OOP II: Inheritance, Interface, Polymorphism, and Abstract
7. Exception Handling
8. Threads
9. Text File Handling
10. Java Database Connectivity (JDBC)
11. Graphical User Interfaces (GUI)
12. Java String API

**Key concepts**

- **Secure** — Java has advanced authentication and access-control features that help make web applications secure.
- **Portable** — Java code runs on all major platforms unmodified — once a source file compiles into bytecode, that bytecode runs on any platform with a Java JDK, unlike languages that must be recompiled into machine code separately for each platform.
- **Robust** — Java has strong memory management and exception-handling features that catch errors during execution and manage incorrect input.
- **Object-Oriented** — A model of programming built around real-world entities — inheritance, data hiding, polymorphism. OOP's aim is to bind a portion of data and the functions that act on it together, so no other part of the code can access them directly.
- **Multithreaded** — Java supports multithreaded programming, so a Java program can perform several tasks at the same time.
- **Architecture-Neutral** — Compiling Java code produces bytecode that runs on many platforms with the help of the Java Runtime Environment (JRE) and Java Virtual Machine (JVM).
- **Interpreted** — Java creates an intermediate representation called bytecode, which is what lets it run on any platform via the JDK.
- **High-Performance** — Java uses a Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler, which converts bytecode instructions to enable faster execution.
- **Distributed** — Java programs can access files on any machine on the internet using RMI and EJB, enabling distributed applications.
- **Dynamic** — Java can compile and load a class dynamically, on demand — only the specifically required portion of code, rather than the whole program.
- **Variables in Java** — A variable in Java is a human-readable name used to store data in computer memory — it lets a program store, read, and change data held in memory. A variable is also called an identifier, because it identifies values within a program.
- **Primitive** — Uses a small, fixed amount of memory to represent a single item of data. Java has exactly eight: `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `char`, and `boolean` — a Java program cannot define any others. Primitives are used so often that making them full objects would noticeably hurt performance.
- **Object (Non-Primitive)** — A larger chunk of memory that can hold a great deal of data along with the methods used to process it. Every data member and local variable must be declared as either a primitive or an object (class) type.
- **char** — A 16-bit character using the Unicode encoding scheme.
- **Conditional execution** — The most common use of the "if-else" statement is to conditionally execute a block of code based on the result of a Boolean expression. For example, you might want to execute a block of code that performs a calculation only if a certain variable has a specific value.
- **Decision making** — The "if-else" statement can also be used to make decisions in your code based on different conditions. For example, you might use an "if-else" statement to determine which of two different actions to take based on the value of a variable.
- **Error checking** — The "if-else" statement can also be used to check for errors or invalid inputs in your code. For example, you might use an "if-else" statement to validate user input and display an error message if the input is not valid.
- **Multiple branches** — The "if-else" statement can also be used to handle multiple branches of execution based on different conditions. For example, you might use multiple "if-else" statements to handle different cases in a switch statement.
- **Initialization expression** — In the above example, int i = 1; is our initialization expression. In this expression we initialize the loop variable to some value so that the loop will start from the initialized value. In the above example the loop will start from 1 and continue to execute until it crosses the value 5.
- **Test expression** — In the above example, i <= 5; is our test expression. The compiler will test the condition written in the test expression. If the condition evaluates to true, then the body of the loop will execute.
- **Step or increment** — This part updates the expression. In the above example, i = i + 1 is our update expression. After executing the body of the loop, the update expression increments the loop variable i by 1 and then moves to test the condition written in the test expression.
- **Built-in Methods** — These methods are predefined, and we can use them any time we want in our Java program. For example pow(), sqrt(), min(), etc.
- **User Defined Methods** — These methods are defined or created by the programmer for performing a specific task in a program.
- **public** — When we declare class members as public, they are accessible from outside the class.
- **private** — When we declare class members as private, they are only accessible within the class and are not accessible from outside the class.
- **default** — When we declare class members with no access specifier is considered as default, they are only accessible within the package and are not accessible from outside the package.
- **protected** — When we declare class members as protected, they are only accessible by any class within the same package or by any subclasses of the parent class in which the class members are declared as protected, regardless of whether the subclass is in the same package or a different package.

### CSC 223 — Discrete Structures

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/csc-223
- 2 units · 200 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: undergraduates across University of Uyo programmes (foundation course, not departmental)

The mathematics of discrete objects — counting, graphs, trees, recurrence relations and Boolean algebra. Graph theory in particular is the direct foundation for network analysis, recommendation systems and the web-data work in UUY-DTS 311.

**Outline**

1. Review of sets, relations and functions in a computing context
2. Propositional and predicate logic; logical equivalence and inference
3. Proof techniques: induction and strong induction; recursive definitions
4. Counting: the product and sum rules, permutations, combinations, the pigeonhole principle
5. Binomial coefficients and combinatorial identities; inclusion–exclusion
6. Recurrence relations and their solution; the Master theorem informally
7. Graph theory: graphs, digraphs, degree, paths, cycles, connectivity
8. Graph representations (adjacency matrix and list), traversal, shortest paths, spanning trees
9. Trees: rooted trees, binary trees, traversal; Boolean algebra and logic circuit minimisation

**Recommended textbooks**

- Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications — Kenneth H. Rosen
- Discrete Mathematics with Applications — Susanna S. Epp

**How to pass**

- Counting problems are deceptively hard — do many, and always ask "does order matter?" and "is repetition allowed?" before choosing a formula
- Graph theory is the highest-value topic for a data scientist here: social networks, web link structures and recommendation graphs are all this
- Recurrence relations explain the running time of recursive algorithms from COS 221 — study the two courses together
- Rosen's exercises are the best preparation for the exam; work them rather than re-reading notes

### CYB 222 — Cybersecurity Innovation and New Technologies

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-222
- 2 units · 200 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Emerging technologies and their cybersecurity implications: AI in security, blockchain, quantum computing threats to cryptography, zero-trust architecture, and the innovation lifecycle in the security industry.

**Outline**

1. AI and machine learning in threat detection
2. Blockchain technology and its security properties
3. Quantum computing and the threat to current cryptography
4. Zero-trust architecture: principles and implementation
5. Security automation: SOAR platforms overview
6. Emerging threat vectors: deepfakes, AI-generated attacks
7. Security innovation lifecycle and technology adoption
8. Open-source intelligence (OSINT) modern tools

**Recommended textbooks**

- AI and Machine Learning for Coders — Laurence Moroney
- Blockchain Basics — Daniel Drescher

**How to pass**

- Stay current — this course changes rapidly; subscribe to a cybersecurity newsletter (SANS, Dark Reading)
- Zero trust ("never trust, always verify") is a major industry direction — understand it thoroughly
- Quantum threats to RSA and AES connect directly to your Cryptography course in 300L
- For exam essays, structure answers around: what the technology is, its security benefit, and its risk

**Lecture notes** (12 transcribed topics; full text needs a free account)

1. AI & Machine Learning in Threat Detection
2. Zero Trust Architecture
3. Post-Quantum Cryptography & Migration Frameworks
4. Behavioral Biometrics & Continuous Authentication
5. Blockchain Technology
6. Cloud Native Security
7. Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PET)
8. Automated Vulnerability Research
9. Agentic AI
10. Deepfake Detection
11. Secure Access Service Edge (SASE)
12. Extended Detection and Response (XDR)

**Key concepts**

- **Abstract** — Traditional security relied on signature-based detection, matching known attack patterns against incoming data — an approach that fails against the rapid evolution of cyberattacks. AI and ML fundamentally change threat detection by letting systems learn from data, recognise behavioural anomalies, and adapt to emerging…
- **Supervised Learning** — Trained on labelled normal/malicious data — spam filtering, malware classification, IDS, fraud. Algorithms: Decision Trees, Random Forest, SVM, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes.
- **Unsupervised Learning** — Finds hidden patterns in unlabelled data for anomaly detection and user-behaviour analytics. Techniques: K-Means, PCA, Autoencoders, density-based clustering.
- **Deep Learning** — Neural networks for large, complex datasets — malware detection, traffic classification, advanced IDS. Models: CNN, RNN, LSTM, Transformers.
- **— Marsh** — Stephen Paul Marsh formalises trust as a computational concept.
- **— Jericho Forum** — Forms to address "de-perimeterisation" of the enterprise network.
- **— Kindervag** — Coins "Zero Trust" at Forrester: trust itself is a vulnerability.
- **/ 2014 — Google BeyondCorp** — Implements then publishes Zero Trust after Operation Aurora; becomes the enterprise blueprint.
- **— NIST SP 800-207** — First comprehensive government-endorsed ZTA framework.
- **— Executive Order 14028** — Mandates Zero Trust for all US federal agencies.
- **— CISA ZTMM v2.0** — Zero Trust Maturity Model across five pillars.
- **Never Trust, Always Verify** — Every request is authenticated and continuously, contextually re-verified — not a one-time login.
- **Least Privilege Access** — Access is scoped, time-limited, and contextual, shrinking the blast radius of any compromise.
- **Assume Breach** — Design as if attackers are already inside: encrypt everything, segment, monitor, and plan recovery.
- **Micro-Segmentation** — Divide the network into isolated segments — down to individual workloads — to contain lateral movement.
- **Identity & Access Management (IAM)** — Identity — not network location — is the primary security boundary; SSO, RBAC, ABAC, risk-based auth.
- **Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)** — Two or more factors (know / have / are); mandatory for sensitive access; adaptive to risk.
- **Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA)** — Replaces VPNs — grants access to specific resources, not the whole network.
- **Device Trust & EDR** — Verifies device health and compliance before access; EDR/MDM monitor and can quarantine endpoints.
- **Data Security & Encryption** — Classify data; encrypt in transit (TLS/SSL) and at rest; DLP and attribute-based access control.
- **SIEM & UEBA** — Aggregate and correlate logs; ML baselines behaviour and flags anomalies — the monitoring backbone.
- **What Is a Quantum Computer?** — A quantum computer is a different computational paradigm, exploiting superposition, entanglement and interference. Where a classical bit is 0 or 1, a qubit can be both at once, so n qubits represent 2ⁿ states simultaneously.
- **Analogy — The Maze** — A classical computer searches a maze one path at a time: hit a dead end, backtrack, try again. A quantum computer, through superposition, effectively evaluates many paths at once and converges exponentially faster.
- **Mosca's Theorem — Quantifying the Urgency** — If (Migration Time) + (Data Secrecy Lifetime) > (Years until Q-Day), the organisation is already at risk. Applied to UNIUYO: a 7-year migration plus a 20-year record-confidentiality requirement = 27 years of protection needed against an ~8-year window.
- **ML-KEM (FIPS 203)** — Primary KEM replacing RSA/Diffie-Hellman; from CRYSTALS-Kyber; ML-KEM-768 recommended; ~17× faster than ECDH on a Cortex-M0+ with 94% less energy; live by default in Google Chrome TLS 1.3
- **ML-DSA (FIPS 204)** — Primary signature replacing ECDSA/RSA; from CRYSTALS-Dilithium; signatures 2,420–4,627 bytes (38–72× larger than ECDSA); rejection sampling causes variable signing latency
- **SLH-DSA (FIPS 205)** — Stateless hash-based signature from SPHINCS+; the suite's insurance policy; very large signatures (7,856–49,856 bytes); for low-frequency, high-security signing
- **Falcon (FIPS 206)** — Compact lattice (NTRU) signature ~666 bytes — best for DNS; hard to implement (constant-time floating-point) and the highest side-channel risk

19. Network Anomaly Detection (K-Means Clustering)
20. The k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) Algorithm
21. Anomaly Detection Using Pandas and Scikit-Learn Libraries
22. Practical Illustration of Anomaly Detection in Customer Credit Card
23. Security Management and Its Objectives
24. The Security Design Process and the Security Management Life Cycle
25. Information Security Policy, Principles and Methodologies
26. Big Data Stages, Technologies and Adoption

**Key concepts**

- **Definition** — Big Data Security refers to the tools, policies, and measures used to protect large volumes of data from unauthorized access, breaches, and misuse throughout its lifecycle — from collection to processing and storage.
- **M2M (Machine to Machine)** — Data exchanged between connected devices
- **People to Machine** — Data generated through human interactions with technology
- **Organisational Data** — Data produced by businesses and institutions
- **Operational Big Data** — Operational Big Data refers to real or nearly real-time data used to support daily business operations and decision making. It processes data immediately as it is generated, supports transactional systems, and requires fast processing.
- **Analytical Big Data** — Analytical Big Data refers to historical and accumulated data used for analysis, forecasting, reporting, and strategic decision making. It focuses on past and current data, supports business intelligence, and is often stored in data warehouses.
- **Technical Skills** — Programming, database management, big data frameworks
- **Analytical Skills** — Data analysis, pattern recognition, statistical analysis
- **Business Skills** — Translating insights into actionable business strategies
- **Communication Skills** — Presenting findings clearly to non-technical audiences
- **Problem Solving Skills** — Using data-driven approaches to solve complex problems
- **Programming** — Ability to write code to manipulate and process data
- **Database Skills** — MySQL, Oracle — querying and managing structured data
- **Big Data Frameworks** — Hadoop, Spark, Kafka — large-scale data processing tools
- **Data sources** — Records the university already holds: semester results and GPA history per course, lecture attendance registers, student-portal login and activity logs, library borrowing and e-resource access, JAMB and O-level entry scores, departmental and level enrolment figures, fee-payment timing, and student feedback or…
- **Collection and storage** — Most of this starts on paper or in departmental spreadsheets, so the first tasks are digitising it and agreeing one student identifier that works across departments. Structured records go into a central data warehouse; feedback text and portal logs suit a data lake.
- **Type of analytics** — All four, in order. Descriptive answers what happened — pass rates by course and level. Diagnostic asks why — which factors track with failure. Predictive identifies which students are likely to carry over a course while there is still time to act. Prescriptive recommends which intervention to offer whom
- **Tools and technology** — Python with pandas for the analysis, PostgreSQL or MySQL for the warehouse, and Power BI or Excel for dashboards that deans will actually open. Hadoop and Spark are the fashionable answer and the wrong one here: a single university produces gigabytes, not petabytes, and one relational database server handles that…
- **Benefits and challenges** — Benefits: at-risk students identified before they carry over a course, better lecturer and timetable allocation, and evidence to support accreditation. Challenges: incomplete and inconsistent records, no single student identifier across departments, staff with no analytics training, unreliable power and connectivity…
- **Volume** — Protecting petabytes or exabytes of data requires security tools that can scale dynamically without creating processing bottlenecks.
- **Velocity** — Data streams into systems in real-time (e.g., IoT sensors, network logs). Security mechanisms like encryption and threat detection must happen on the fly without causing latency.
- **Variety** — Big Data includes structured SQL databases, semi-structured JSON files, and unstructured data like video, audio, and text. A one-size-fits-all security policy does not work here.
- **Encryption in Transit** — Protecting data as it moves between nodes, clusters, or users (typically using TLS/SSL).
- **Encryption at Rest** — Safeguarding data stored on disks using strong encryption standards (like AES-256).
- **Data Masking & Tokenization** — Replacing sensitive data (like credit card numbers or PII) with realistic but fake data or tokens before it enters the analytics pipeline so data scientists can work with it safely.
- **Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)** — Assigning permissions based on organizational roles.
- **Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)** — A finer-grained approach where access is determined by contextual attributes (e.g., "Allow access only if the user is a Data Analyst AND the request comes from an internal IP during working hours").
- **Node Authentication** — Ensuring that only authorized servers/nodes can join the computing cluster (often managed via Kerberos).

### DTS 224 — Statistical Inference and Modelling

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-224
- 3 units · 200 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Reasoning from a sample to a population: estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and the linear model. The core statistical machinery of the degree — and the part most often misused in practice.

**Outline**

1. Populations, samples, parameters and statistics; sampling distributions
2. The Central Limit Theorem and its practical consequences
3. Point estimation: unbiasedness, efficiency, consistency; method of moments and maximum likelihood
4. Interval estimation: confidence intervals for means, proportions and variances
5. Hypothesis testing: null and alternative hypotheses, test statistics, p-values, Type I and Type II errors, power
6. One- and two-sample tests: z, t, chi-square and F tests
7. Analysis of variance (ANOVA): one-way and two-way
8. Simple and multiple linear regression: estimation, interpretation, inference on coefficients
9. Model diagnostics: residual analysis, multicollinearity, and the assumptions of the linear model

**Recommended textbooks**

- Mathematical Statistics with Applications — Wackerly, Mendenhall & Scheaffer
- Statistical Inference — George Casella & Roger L. Berger
- OpenIntro Statistics — Diez, Çetinkaya-Rundel & Barr

**How to pass**

- Learn what a p-value actually is and — more importantly — what it is not. Almost everyone gets this wrong, and examiners specifically test the misinterpretations
- A confidence interval is a statement about the procedure, not about the parameter. Say it correctly once and it stays right forever
- Simulate the Central Limit Theorem yourself in R (DTS 211): draw 1000 samples, plot the means, watch it become normal. Nothing else makes it as concrete
- For every test, memorise the assumptions alongside the formula — "which test do I use here?" is the exam's favourite question

### DTS 226 — Probability for Data Science

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-226
- 3 units · 200 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The mathematics of uncertainty: probability axioms, random variables, distributions, expectation, and the limit theorems. Probability is the language machine learning is written in — every model output is ultimately a probability statement.

**Outline**

1. Sample spaces, events and the axioms of probability
2. Conditional probability, independence, the law of total probability and Bayes' theorem
3. Discrete random variables: probability mass functions, expectation and variance
4. Discrete distributions: Bernoulli, binomial, geometric, hypergeometric, Poisson
5. Continuous random variables: density and distribution functions
6. Continuous distributions: uniform, exponential, gamma, normal
7. Joint, marginal and conditional distributions; covariance and correlation
8. Transformations of random variables; moment generating functions
9. Laws of large numbers and the Central Limit Theorem; introduction to Markov chains

**Recommended textbooks**

- A First Course in Probability — Sheldon Ross
- Introduction to Probability — Blitzstein & Hwang

**How to pass**

- Bayes' theorem is the most important single formula in the course — it is the entire basis of Naive Bayes classifiers and of Bayesian inference
- Watch Joe Blitzstein's Stat 110 lectures (free on YouTube); they are the best probability teaching available anywhere
- For each distribution, learn the story that generates it ("number of successes in n trials", "waiting time until first event") — then you never have to guess which one applies
- Draw the sample space for small problems. Most probability mistakes are modelling mistakes, not arithmetic mistakes

### ENT 221 — Entrepreneurship and Innovation

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/ent-221
- 2 units · 200 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: undergraduates across University of Uyo programmes (foundation course, not departmental)

Business thinking for technical students: entrepreneurship and intrapreneurship theory, entrepreneurial characteristics and thinking, innovation, enterprise formation, and e-commerce principles. Directly applicable to consulting, startup, and freelance careers in technology.

**Outline**

1. Concept of entrepreneurship and intrapreneurship/corporate entrepreneurship
2. Theories, rationale and relevance: Schumpeterian perspective, risk-taking, creative destruction
3. Characteristics of entrepreneurs: opportunity seeker, risk taker, innovator
4. Entrepreneurial thinking: critical, reflective, and creative thinking
5. Innovation: concept, dimensions, and its relationship to knowledge and change
6. Enterprise formation, partnership and networking: business plans, ownership forms, registration

9. Basic principles of e-commerce

- The Lean Startup — Eric Ries

**How to pass**

- Apply every concept to a technology business idea from your own field — it makes abstract topics concrete and exam-ready
- The Business Model Canvas is the most exam-critical framework — practise filling it in for different scenarios
- Nigeria's NITDA and other agencies offer technology grants — research them as part of your learning
- This course matters for your career: many technology professionals eventually consult or freelance

**Lecture notes** (18 transcribed topics; full text needs a free account)

1. The Concept of Entrepreneurship

18. Contemporary Issues in Entrepreneurship

**Key concepts**

- **Who is an “Entrepreneur?”** — An entrepreneur is an individual who identifies an opportunity and organizes the necessary resources to exploit it. This definition highlights two key aspects of entrepreneurship: opportunity recognition and resource mobilization.
- **Creativity and Innovation** — The ability to think outside the box and develop new solutions to problems.
- **Resilience and Perseverance** — The capacity to bounce back from failure and keep going in the face of obstacles.
- **Self-Confidence** — A strong belief in one's abilities and the value of one's ideas.
- **Vision** — The ability to see the big picture and anticipate future trends.
- **Need for Achievement** — A strong drive to succeed and reach one's goals.
- **The Concept and Meaning of Entrepreneurship** — Entrepreneurship is a multifaceted concept that can be understood from various perspectives. At its core, it is the process of creating value by bringing together a unique package of resources to exploit an opportunity.
- **The Concept of Intrapreneurship** — Intrapreneurship, also known as corporate entrepreneurship, refers to the practice of fostering an entrepreneurial mindset and behaviors within an established organization. It involves encouraging employees to think and act like entrepreneurs, identifying and pursuing new opportunities that can drive growth and…
- **Corporate Entrepreneurship Defined** — Corporate entrepreneurship is a broad term that encompasses a variety of activities aimed at fostering innovation and growth within an established firm. It can be defined as the process by which teams within an established company conceive, foster, launch and manage a new business that is distinct from the parent…
- **Corporate Venturing** — This involves the creation of new businesses by an established firm. This can be done through internal corporate venturing, where the new business is developed within the company, or external corporate venturing, where the company invests in or partners with outside startups.
- **Strategic Entrepreneurship** — This refers to a firm's efforts to achieve creativity and innovation in its strategic areas, such as its business model, product services, or served markets. It involves using entrepreneurial thinking to gain a competitive advantage and drive long-term growth.
- **Entrepreneurial Mindset and Behaviours** — It is not a big idea alone that paves the path to ultimate entrepreneurial success; the mindset and behaviour of the "would-be" entrepreneur plays a crucial role. Entrepreneurs are often seen as innovators, risk-takers, and visionaries who create value and solve problems in the world, but what makes them different…
- **Challenges in Developing an Entrepreneurial Mindset** — The mind is often regarded as the most powerful attribute and weapon every human has. Whatever we become is always attributed to the state of our mind. Thus, developing an enterprise is chiefly a function of the state of our mind and that is where the battle for life and success began.
- **Overcoming the Fear of Failure** — One of the primary hurdles to fostering an entrepreneurial mindset is surmounting the fear of failure. Many individuals shy away from taking risks and initiating their ventures due to concerns about potential negative consequences.
- **Cultivating Self-Confidence** — Entrepreneurs must possess unwavering self-confidence in their abilities to navigate the uncertainties of the business world. A lack of self-confidence can impede decision-making processes and create obstacles to pursuing new opportunities.
- **Embracing Change** — Entrepreneurship is synonymous with change, innovation, and continuous learning. Those resistant to change may find it challenging to adapt to new situations and acquire the necessary skills for success.
- **Managing Uncertainty** — The inherent uncertainty of entrepreneurship makes decision-making challenging without knowing the outcome. Developing a tolerance for uncertainty is crucial, requiring the ability to make informed decisions despite limited information.
- **Financial Stability Concerns** — Commencing a new venture often involves financial risks, and the apprehension of financial instability can hinder the development of an entrepreneurial mindset. Mitigating these concerns involves careful financial planning, risk assessment, and a strategic approach to resource allocation.
- **Building a Supportive Ecosystem** — Entrepreneurs thrive in supportive environments with access to resources like funding, mentorship, and networking opportunities. The absence of such support can hinder the development of necessary skills and knowledge for success.
- **Balancing Work and Life** — Entrepreneurs often grapple with long working hours and challenges in maintaining a healthy work-life balance. Managing personal well-being and relationships while pursuing a new venture requires intentional efforts to prioritize self-care, set boundaries, and cultivate resilience amidst the demands of…
- **Resilience to Criticism and Rejection** — Entrepreneurs frequently encounter criticism, rejection, and skepticism from others. Developing resilience and the ability to persevere despite criticism is crucial for success. Fortifying mental strength involves reframing criticism as constructive feedback, learning from setbacks, and maintaining a steadfast focus…
- **Sustaining Motivation and Perseverance** — The entrepreneurial journey is a protracted and challenging endeavor. Sustaining motivation, focus, and perseverance is vital, especially during setbacks and obstacles. Entrepreneurs must cultivate a resilient mindset, set achievable milestones, and celebrate small victories to stay motivated on the path to long-term…
- **Fostering Creative and Innovative Thinking** — Entrepreneurship demands creative problem-solving and innovative thinking. Developing these skills can be challenging, particularly for individuals with traditional educational or professional backgrounds.
- **Rationale and Relevance of Entrepreneurship** — Entrepreneurship as we see has to do with the persistent of opportunity to create wealth through innovative creation of product or service that meets a need of customers, using scarce resources in any way that result in enterprise development and growth which satisfies the expectation of stakeholders whose roles…
- **Creation of Employment** — It has been pointed out at various times and with varying degrees of emphasis that entrepreneurship creates employment for the teaming population of any nation. In Nigeria, for instance, it is documented that small and medium scale business, the catalyst of entrepreneurship employs about 30% of the entire labour force…
- **Transformation of Traditional Industry** — Entrepreneurial activities help to transform the traditional sector thereby helping in the economic development of a nation. In one respect, it helps in modernizing the people's perception of life, and in another, it modernizes the traditional handicraft prevalent in the rural economies, by introducing the use of…
- **Utilization of Resources** — Entrepreneurship helps to mobilize resources that would otherwise remain idle in the lands of people and employ them productively. By so doing, capital formation which is a vital engine of economic growth is encouraged.
- **Better Standard of Living** — As a result of their numerous economic activities, entrepreneurship activities make large quantities of goods and services available to people. With increased supply of goods and services individual's demands increase as well. This increase in demand, in turn, results in a better standard of living for the people.

### INS 224 — Systems Analysis and Design

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/ins-224
- 3 units · 200 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: undergraduates across University of Uyo programmes (foundation course, not departmental)

A structured approach to analysing information system needs and designing solutions: the software development lifecycle, top-down and bottom-up design, dataflow diagramming, entity-relationship modelling, and file/database and user-interface design.

**Outline**

1. Structured approach to analysis and design of information systems for businesses
2. Software development lifecycle (SDLC)
3. Structured top-down and bottom-up design
4. Dataflow diagramming and entity-relationship modelling
5. Computer-aided software engineering (CASE)
6. Input/output, prototyping design and validation
7. File and database design
8. Design of user interfaces
9. Comparison of structured and object-oriented design

**Recommended textbooks**

- Systems Analysis and Design — Kenneth Kendall & Julie Kendall
- Modern Systems Analysis and Design — Hoffer, George & Valacich

**How to pass**

- DFDs and ER diagrams are the most commonly examined topics — practise drawing them from scratch
- Use DRAW.IO (free, online) to practise system diagrams until speed and accuracy improve
- Normalisation (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) has a logical pattern — understand it conceptually before memorising rules
- Relate everything to a real system you interact with (a bank app, university portal) to aid understanding

**Lecture notes** (27 transcribed topics; full text needs a free account)

1. Introduction to Systems Analysis and Design
2. Feasibility Study in Systems Analysis and Design
3. The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)
4. Software Development Life Cycle Models — Overview
5. The Waterfall Model
6. The V-Model
7. Iterative Models
8. The Incremental Model
9. Evolutionary Process Models
10. The Spiral Model
11. The Prototyping Model
12. The Agile Model
13. Comparison of SDLC Models
14. Requirement Analysis
15. System Modeling Overview & Structured Analysis
16. Data Flow Diagrams (DFD)
17. Business Process Modeling Notation (BPMN)
18. Entity Relationship Diagrams (ERD)
19. Decision Tables and Decision Trees
20. Introduction to UML
21. Use Case Diagrams
22. Class Diagrams
23. Sequence Diagrams
24. Activity Diagrams
25. State Chart Diagrams
26. Component Diagrams
27. Deployment Diagrams

**Key concepts**

- **Business to Consumer (B2C)** — A computerized system that facilitates the exchange of products, services, and information directly between businesses and individual consumers through the internet.
- **Business to Business (B2B)** — A computerized information system that supports the exchange of information, products, services, and transactions between business organizations through the internet to improve operational efficiency and collaboration.
- **Break-Even Analysis** — Determines when cumulative benefits equal cumulative costs.
- **Return on Investment (ROI)** — Measures the financial return relative to the cost of investment.
- **Net Present Value (NPV)** — Accounts for the time value of money when comparing future benefits against current costs.
- **Payback Period** — Estimates how long before the investment is recovered.
- **User acceptance** — The degree to which users willingly adopt and correctly use the system.
- **Management support** — Projects without visible leadership endorsement often fail at the implementation stage.
- **Training requirements** — Complex systems require substantial training investment.
- **Impact on jobs** — Systems that threaten job security or significantly change job roles may face strong resistance.
- **Data protection and privacy laws** — Systems that store or process personal data must comply with relevant legislation (e.g., Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, GDPR for European-facing systems).
- **Intellectual property** — Software components, databases, or algorithms used in the system must be properly licensed.
- **Industry-specific regulations** — Financial systems must comply with banking regulations; healthcare systems must meet patient confidentiality standards.
- **Contract obligations** — Existing vendor contracts may restrict the ability to switch platforms or integrate third-party tools.
- **Employment law** — Systems that monitor employee activity (e.g., keystroke logging) may face legal scrutiny.
- **Gantt Charts** — Bar charts that map tasks against a timeline, showing start and end dates and task dependencies.
- **PERT (Programme Evaluation and Review Technique)** — Analyses task durations probabilistically to estimate overall project duration.
- **Critical Path Method (CPM)** — Identifies the longest sequence of dependent tasks that determines the minimum project duration.
- **Technical feasibility** — Does the required technology exist? Does the team have the skills?
- **Economic feasibility** — Will the benefits justify the costs? What is the expected return on investment (ROI)?
- **Operational feasibility** — Will the intended users accept and use the system?
- **Legal/ethical feasibility** — Are there regulatory or ethical constraints?
- **Functional Requirements** — This is what the system does, its behaviours, features, and functions. For example, "The system shall allow users to reset their password via email."
- **Non-Functional Requirements** — Non-functional requirements encompass performance, security, reliability, scalability, usability, and maintainability, among others. This tells how well the system performs, using quality attributes. For example, "The system shall respond to any user request within 2 seconds under normal load."
- **Interviews** — One-on-one discussions with users, managers, or domain experts.
- **Surveys and questionnaires** — Useful when stakeholders are numerous or geographically dispersed.
- **Observation (ethnographic study)** — Watching users perform their current tasks to understand workflows and pain points.
- **Workshops and focus groups** — Bringing multiple stakeholders together to collaboratively define needs.

### MTH 223 — Introduction to Numerical Analysis

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/mth-223
- 2 units · 200 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: undergraduates across University of Uyo programmes (foundation course, not departmental)

How to compute answers to mathematical problems that have no closed-form solution, and how to know when the computed answer is wrong. Error, convergence and stability — the reason floating-point arithmetic sometimes betrays you.

**Outline**

1. Sources of error: round-off, truncation, and floating-point representation
2. Absolute, relative and percentage error; error propagation and conditioning
3. Solution of nonlinear equations: bisection, false position, Newton–Raphson, secant method
4. Convergence criteria and rates of convergence
5. Solution of linear systems: Gaussian elimination, LU decomposition, pivoting
6. Iterative methods: Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel
7. Interpolation: Lagrange and Newton divided-difference polynomials; spline interpolation
8. Numerical differentiation and integration: trapezoidal rule, Simpson's rules
9. Numerical solution of ordinary differential equations: Euler and Runge–Kutta methods

**Recommended textbooks**

- Numerical Analysis — Richard L. Burden & J. Douglas Faires
- Numerical Methods in Engineering with Python 3 — Jaan Kiusalaas

**How to pass**

- Implement every method in Python as you learn it — a method you have coded is a method you understand
- Newton–Raphson is the same algorithm family as gradient descent; recognising that makes UUY-DTS 313 far less mysterious
- Learn WHY floating-point comparison with == is unsafe; this single fact prevents a whole class of real bugs in data pipelines
- Exam questions usually ask for two or three iterations by hand — practise tabulating iterations neatly and carrying enough decimal places

### UUY-CYB 221 — Network Defense Fundamentals

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-cyb-221
- 2 units · 200 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Practical network security: identification/authentication/authorization, threat classification, firewalls, administrative/physical/technical controls, virtualization and cloud, wireless/mobile/IoT security, and cryptography/PKI. Builds directly on the networking foundation from UUY-CYB 121.

**Outline**

1. Network security fundamentals; identification, authentication and authorization
2. Classification of threats: malware, intrusions, denial of service
3. Fundamentals of firewalls and implementation approaches
4. Network security controls: administrative, physical, and technical
5. Virtualization and cloud computing security
6. Wireless network security, mobile device security, and IoT device security
7. Data security: cryptography and public key infrastructure (PKI)
8. Network traffic monitoring; basic network utilities (ipconfig, ping, tracert, netstat)

**Recommended textbooks**

- Network Security Essentials — William Stallings
- CompTIA CySA+ Study Guide — Mike Chapple & David Seidl

**How to pass**

- Install Wireshark (free) and capture your own network traffic — hands-on analysis builds intuition fast
- Use Cisco Packet Tracer (free) to build and defend virtual networks before exams
- Know the difference between IDS (detect only) and IPS (detect + block) — exam-critical
- Relate every defence mechanism to a specific attack from UUY-CYB 212 — show the attack/defence pairing

**Lecture notes** (21 transcribed topics; full text needs a free account)

1. Threats, Vulnerabilities and the CIA Triad
2. Malware, Hardware Attacks and Threat Categories
3. Firewalls
4. Network Foundations: OSI, TCP/IP and Connection Setup
5. Classical Network Attacks
6. Encryption Controls and Virtual Private Networks

10. Practical 1: Strings, Files and Basic Network Communication
11. Practical 2: Basic Encryption and Decryption Algorithms

14. Practical 5: Client-Server Application and Socket Programming
15. Practical 6: Live Packet Analysis
16. Practical 7: Creating a Web Scraper to Gather Data from Websites
17. Practical 8: Simple Penetration Testing Tasks
18. Practical 9: Scripts for Basic Static Malware Analysis
19. Practical 10: Intrusion Detection and Traffic Monitoring
20. Practical 11: Threat Detection
21. Practical 12: Firewall Screening of Incoming and Outgoing Packets

**Key concepts**

- **Classification of Threats** — A cyber-attack is an exploitation of computer systems and networks. It uses malicious code to alter computer code, logic or data and lead to cybercrimes, such as information and identity theft.
- **Injection attacks** — It is the attack in which some data will be injected into a web application to manipulate the application and fetch the required information. Example- SQL Injection, code Injection, log Injection, XML Injection etc.
- **DNS Spoofing** — DNS Spoofing is a type of computer security hacking. Whereby a data is introduced into a DNS resolver’s cache causing the name server to return an incorrect IP address, diverting traffic to the attacker’s computer or any other computer.
- **Session Hijacking** — It is a security attack on a user session over a protected network. Web applications create cookies to store the state and user sessions. By stealing the cookies, an attacker can have access to all of the user data.
- **Phishing** — Phishing is a type of attack which attempts to steal sensitive information like user login credentials and credit card number. It occurs when an attacker is masquerading as a trustworthy entity in electronic communication.
- **Brute force** — It is a type of attack which uses a trial-and-error method. This attack generates a large number of guesses and validates them to obtain actual data like user password and personal identification number.
- **Denial of Service** — It is an attack which meant to make a server or network resource unavailable to the users. It accomplishes this by flooding the target with traffic or sending it information that triggers a crash. It uses the single system and single internet connection to attack a server. It can be classified into the following-
- **Dictionary attacks** — This type of attack stored the list of a commonly used password and validated them to get original password.
- **URL Interpretation** — It is a type of attack where we can change the certain parts of a URL, and one can make a web server to deliver web pages for which he is not authorized to browse.
- **File Inclusion attacks** — It is a type of attack that allows an attacker to access unauthorized or essential files which is available on the web server or to execute malicious files on the web server by making use of the include functionality.
- **Man in the middle attacks** — It is a type of attack that allows an attacker to intercepts the connection between client and server and acts as a bridge between them. Due to this, an attacker will be able to read, insert and modify the data in the intercepted connection.
- **Virus** — It is a type of malicious software program that spread throughout the computer files without the knowledge of a user. It is a self-replicating malicious computer program that replicates by inserting copies of itself into other computer programs when executed.
- **Worm** — It is a type of malware whose primary function is to replicate itself to spread to uninfected computers. It works same as the computer virus. Worms often originate from email attachments that appear to be from trusted senders.
- **Trojan horse** — It is a malicious program that occurs unexpected changes to computer setting and unusual activity, even when the computer should be idle. It misleads the user of its true intent. It appears to be a normal application but when opened/executed some malicious code will run in the background.
- **Backdoors** — It is a method that bypasses the normal authentication process. A developer may create a backdoor so that an application or operating system can be accessed for troubleshooting or other purposes.
- **Bots** — A bot (short for "robot") is an automated process that interacts with other network services. Some bots program run automatically, while others only execute commands when they receive specific input. Common examples of bots program are the crawler, chatroom bots, and malicious bots.
- **The 7 Layers of Cyber Security** — The 7 layers of cyber security should Centre on the mission critical assets you are seeking to protect.
- **Vulnerability, Threat, Harmful Acts** — As the recent epidemic of data breaches illustrates, no system is immune to attacks. Any company that manages, transmits, stores, or otherwise handles data has to institute and enforce mechanisms to monitor their cyber environment, identify vulnerabilities, and close up security holes as quickly as possible.
- **CIA Triad** — The CIA Triad is actually a security model that has been developed to help people think about various parts of IT security.
- **Assets and Threat** — What is an Asset: An asset is any data, device or other component of an organization’s systems that is valuable – often because it contains sensitive data or can be used to access such information.
- **Types of Cyber-Attacker Actions** — Active attacks: An active attack is a network exploit in which a hacker attempts to make changes to data on the target or data en route to the target.
- **Masquerade** — In this attack, the intruder pretends to be a particular user of a system to gain access or to gain greater privileges than they are authorized for. A masquerade may be attempted through the use of stolen login IDs and passwords, through finding security gaps in programs or through bypassing the authentication…
- **Session replay** — In this type of attack, a hacker steals an authorized user’s log in information by stealing the session ID. The intruder gains access and the ability to do anything the authorized user can do on the website.
- **Message modification** — In this attack, an intruder alters packet header addresses to direct a message to a different destination or modify the data on a target machine.
- **Denial of service (DoS)** — In a denial of service (DoS) attack, users are deprived of access to a network or web resource. This is generally accomplished by overwhelming the target with more traffic than it can handle.
- **Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS)** — In a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) exploit, large numbers of compromised systems (sometimes called a botnet or zombie army) attack a single target.
- **Eavesdropping (tapping)** — The attacker simply listens to messages exchanged by two entities. For the attack to be useful, the traffic must not be encrypted. Any unencrypted information, such as a password sent in response to an HTTP request, may be retrieved by the attacker.
- **Traffic analysis** — The attacker looks at the metadata transmitted in traffic in order to deduce information relating to the exchange and the participating entities, e.g. the form of the exchanged traffic (rate, duration, etc.).

### UUY-CYB 222 — Web and Mobile Applications Security

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-cyb-222
- 2 units · 200 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Attacking and defending web and mobile applications. Covers the OWASP Top 10 in depth, secure coding practices for Java/Python/Kotlin/Swift, audit and QA testing, and mobile-specific threats on iOS and Android platforms.

**Outline**

1. The impact of the internet and web applications on the business world
2. Principles and strategies for the design and implementation of secure applications — writing software that makes it difficult for intruders to exploit security loopholes in applications/code
3. Secure program development for mobile (Android, iOS) and web
4. Delineation of web-based risks, common website attacks, weaknesses, and security best practices
5. Value and importance of vulnerability and security assessment for web and mobile applications
6. Attributes and qualities of secure coding practices
7. Role and importance of audit compliance and quality assurance testing for web/mobile applications
8. Next-generation challenges in securing web/mobile applications and data
9. Lifecycle approach to web/mobile application security

**Recommended textbooks**

- The Web Application Hacker's Handbook — Stuttard & Pinto
- Real-World Bug Hunting — Peter Yaworski

**How to pass**

- PortSwigger Web Security Academy is free and has labs for every OWASP Top 10 vulnerability — essential
- DVWA (Damn Vulnerable Web Application) is a free practice target you can run locally
- For every vulnerability, know: how it works, how to exploit it, and how to fix it
- Bug bounty write-ups on HackerOne and Bugcrowd are the best real-world case studies

**Lecture notes** (13 transcribed topics; full text needs a free account)

1. Foundations: Web & Mobile Applications
2. Impact of the Internet & Web Applications on Business
3. Principles & Strategies for Secure Design
4. Mobile Threats & Secure Development Practices
5. Mobile Platform Security Models — iOS vs Android
6. Mobile Bearer Layers — WAP, Bluetooth, SMS/MMS & Location
7. Risks & Threats
8. Website Attacks
9. Strengths, Weaknesses & Best Practice
10. Audit, Compliance & Quality Assurance
11. Web Application Security & the Security Lifecycle
12. The OWASP Top 10 — Ranking Web Application Risk
13. Exam Focus — The Lecturer’s Guaranteed Questions

**Key concepts**

- **Web Application** — A web application is software controlled by a centralized server and accessed through browsers with an internet connection. Web apps use a combination of server-side (e.g. PHP, ASP.NET) and client-side (HTML, CSS) scripts to process and present data to the user.
- **Mobile Application** — A mobile application is software installed directly on a user’s device (iOS or Android), designed to run on a mobile device or tablet. Some mobile apps can also be accessed via an internet connection and a web browser.
- **E-commerce** — E-commerce refers to markets enabled by the internet — the buying and selling of goods and services online.
- **Teleconferencing & Remote Collaboration** — Teleconferencing is the use of digital technology to communicate between businesses or individuals located in different geographical areas.
- **Audio Conferencing** — Communication by voice only, with no video — e.g. a conference phone call
- **Video Conferencing** — Participants see and hear each other in real time — e.g. Zoom or Google Meet
- **Web Conferencing** — Online meetings that add shared screens, slides and documents to the call
- **Hybrid Conferencing** — Combines in-person and remote participants in the same meeting
- **Marketing, Advertising & Customer Engagement** — The internet lets businesses reach and engage customers directly, and much of it is powered by tracking. When a cookie is dropped on a platform, it records that a person searched for a particular item — which lets the business show that person targeted adverts later.
- **Supply Chain & Logistics** — Logistics and supply chain management benefit significantly from internet connectivity and web applications, which coordinate the flow of goods, information and resources.
- **Recreational / “for fun”** — Curiosity or a technical challenge, without intent to cause damage
- **Fame** — The desire for recognition within a hacking community
- **Activism (“hacktivism”)** — Pursuing a political, social, or ideological cause
- **Financial gain** — The most common driver of serious cybercrime — fraud, extortion, data resale
- **Coercion** — An individual is forced or blackmailed into compromising a system
- **Destruction** — Intent to disrupt, delete, or disable systems and data
- **Espionage** — Gathering confidential information for competitive, corporate, or state advantage
- **Hobbyists** — Informal, curiosity-driven individuals, often with limited resources
- **Government & law-enforcement agencies** — Acting under legal authority, though their tools and techniques mirror those of attackers
- **Activists** — Acting in pursuit of a cause rather than personal gain
- **Cyberterrorists** — Seeking to cause fear, disruption, or harm at scale
- **Criminal actors** — Organized groups pursuing financial gain
- **Insiders** — Employees or contractors who already hold legitimate access, making them uniquely positioned to cause damage
- **AI-augmented hackers** — An emerging category using automated and AI-assisted tools to scale reconnaissance and attacks
- **Authentication vs Authorization** — Authentication is the process of verifying the identity of a user, device, or service before granting access to protected digital resources. Authorization is the process of giving a verified user permission to access a physical location or digital information.
- **Password Security & Creation** — Password policy is the most basic layer of access control, and it should be enforced at the point a user or account is created, not applied after the fact.
- **Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)** — 2FA adds a second, independently generated credential on top of the known password. During registration the system collects an alternative contact point — typically a phone number or email address — and at login it sends a one-time code (commonly 4–8 digits) to that channel.
- **Three-Factor Authentication (3FA)** — 3FA requires evidence from three independent categories of proof, not merely three steps or three devices. The three factors are: something you know — a password, PIN or passphrase; something you have — a phone, hardware token or smart card; and something you are — a fingerprint, face or iris.

### UUY-DTS 224 — Programming in Data Science

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-224
- 2 units · 200 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The working Python data stack: NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib and scikit-learn. Where the mathematics of the other 200 Level courses becomes code you can run on a real dataset.

**Outline**

1. The scientific Python ecosystem; notebooks, environments and package management
2. NumPy: ndarrays, dtypes, vectorisation, broadcasting, slicing and linear algebra routines
3. pandas: Series and DataFrame, indexing, selection and filtering
4. Data cleaning in pandas: missing values, type conversion, duplicates, string operations
5. Reshaping and combining data: groupby, pivot, melt, merge and concat
6. Time-series handling: datetime indexes, resampling and rolling windows
7. Visualisation with Matplotlib and Seaborn
8. An introduction to scikit-learn: the estimator API, fit/predict, pipelines
9. Writing reusable code: functions, modules, virtual environments and version control with Git

**Recommended textbooks**

- Python for Data Analysis — Wes McKinney
- Python Data Science Handbook — Jake VanderPlas

**How to pass**

- Learn groupby properly — the split-apply-combine pattern solves an astonishing share of real analysis tasks
- Write vectorised NumPy/pandas code rather than Python loops; on a large dataset the difference is minutes versus hours
- Keep every notebook in Git from day one. Reproducibility is a graded expectation by DTS 417
- Recreate a chart you have seen in a news article using Matplotlib; matching a real design teaches more than following a tutorial

## 300 Level

### CSC 319 — Artificial Intelligence

Foundations of AI: intelligent agents, search algorithms, knowledge representation, semantic networks, natural language processing, and expert systems. Directly relevant to AI-powered anomaly detection, prediction, and automated analysis across computing.

**Outline**

3. Search: general classes of AI search problems, techniques and strategies

- Google's free Machine Learning Crash Course covers supervised/unsupervised ML at the right level
- AI ethics questions (bias, fairness) appear frequently — develop considered, referenced arguments

### CYB 311 — Cryptography Techniques, Algorithms and Applications

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-311
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The mathematical and algorithmic foundations of modern cryptography: symmetric and asymmetric cryptosystems, key management, hash functions, digital signatures, PKI, and protocol security. The theoretical backbone of all secure communications.

**Outline**

1. Introduction to cryptography: symmetric and asymmetric cryptosystems, key management
2. Cryptanalysis; stream ciphers, block ciphers, and Feistel ciphers
3. Hash functions; data integrity, authentication, and perfect secrecy
4. Public-key cryptography and discrete algorithms: ElGamal, algorithmic number theory, primality testing
5. Security of ElGamal and RSA encryption; RSA key generation; discrete logarithm schemes
6. Selected cryptosystems: DES, RSA, and the AES symmetric block cipher
7. PKI, SSL, and VPN
8. Digital signatures, pseudo-random number generation, and cryptographic protocols
9. Certificate authorities; policies and procedures for the proper use of cryptography

**Recommended textbooks**

- Cryptography and Network Security — William Stallings
- Introduction to Modern Cryptography — Katz & Lindell

**How to pass**

- Work through RSA key generation by hand at least twice — the maths is not complex once you step through it
- Know the difference between confidentiality (encryption), integrity (MAC/hash), and authentication (signature)
- Computerphile on YouTube has outstanding, accessible videos on every topic in this course — free
- Quantum threats from this course directly link to CYB 222 (Innovation) and CYB 411 (Vulnerability Assessment)

### CYB 312 — Biometrics Security

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-312
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Biometric authentication systems: digital image/signal processing, matching algorithms, error metrics, and data security. Covers implementation in national identity systems and access control.

**Outline**

1. Introduction to biometrics and digital image processing
2. Biometric algorithms and systems: face, fingerprint, iris, voice
3. Automated biometric identification and multimodal biometrics
4. Biometric data: raw data, template data, and data methods
5. Matching basics: enrolment, match threshold, matching performance
6. Calculating error rates and graphs (FAR, FRR, EER)
7. Storage of biometric data: transactions, quality upgrades, data security and integrity
8. Privacy issues; security strength and recognition rates
9. Applications of biometrics and future trends; alternatives to passwords and smart cards

**Recommended textbooks**

- Biometric System and Data Analysis — Ted Dunstone & Neil Yager

**How to pass**

- FAR vs FRR trade-off is the most examined concept — understand the EER graphically
- Nigeria's NIN (National Identity Number) system is a real-world case study for national biometrics
- Biometric privacy connects to the Nigeria Data Protection Act from CYB 224 — link them
- Presentation attack / spoofing scenarios make excellent exam answers for "practical examples"

### CYB 313 — Cybersecurity Risks Analysis, Challenges and Mitigation

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-313
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Systematic methods for identifying, analysing, and treating cybersecurity risks. Covers applied information security management, risk mitigation in the cloud, governance and security policy, the ISO 27000 series, and the economic/geopolitical factors behind Africa's cyber risk exposure.

**Outline**

1. Principles of applied information security management
2. Cybersecurity risks, challenges, and the path forward; recognizing risks
3. Decision and risk analysis techniques; mitigating risks and vulnerabilities
4. Effective use of assessments for cybersecurity risk mitigation, including in the cloud
5. Economic and geopolitical factors behind Africa's vulnerability to cyber-attacks
6. Governance and security policy; threat and vulnerability management
7. Incident management, risk assessment and risk management frameworks
8. Information leakage, crisis management, and business continuity
9. ISO 27000 series and the Plan-Do-Check-Act model
10. Incident response, forensics, and investigations; legal and regulatory drivers

**Recommended textbooks**

- Risk Analysis and the Security Survey — James F. Broder & Gene Tucker
- CompTIA Security+ Study Guide — Mike Chapple & David Seidl

**How to pass**

- Practise ALE/SLE/ARO calculations until they are automatic — they appear in nearly every exam
- STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, DoS, Elevation) — memorise and apply it to any system
- Risk registers are a practical exam task — practise building one for a sample organisation
- BCP and DR are distinct: BCP keeps the business running, DR recovers IT systems — know the difference

### DTS 312 — Big Data Computing

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-312
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

What changes when the data no longer fits on one machine. Distributed storage and computation, the MapReduce model, Hadoop and Spark, and the architectural patterns of modern data platforms.

**Outline**

1. Characterising big data: volume, velocity, variety, veracity and value
2. Why scale-up fails and scale-out wins; commodity clusters and fault tolerance
3. Distributed file systems: HDFS architecture, blocks, replication, NameNode and DataNodes
4. The MapReduce programming model: map, shuffle, reduce; worked word-count and join examples
5. The Hadoop ecosystem: YARN, Hive, HBase, Sqoop, Flume
6. Apache Spark: RDDs, DataFrames, lazy evaluation, transformations vs actions, in-memory computation
7. Spark SQL and PySpark for data processing
8. Stream processing concepts: Kafka, windowing, and batch vs streaming architectures
9. NoSQL stores and the CAP theorem; cloud big-data services

**Recommended textbooks**

- Hadoop: The Definitive Guide — Tom White
- Learning Spark — Damji, Wenig, Das & Lee
- Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Martin Kleppmann

**How to pass**

- Be able to trace a word-count through map → shuffle → reduce by hand; it is the classic exam question and it teaches the model properly
- Install Spark locally (or use a free Databricks Community workspace) and run PySpark on a few million rows — the concepts stay abstract until you see a job execute
- Understand WHY Spark is faster than MapReduce (in-memory, DAG scheduling, lazy evaluation) rather than just asserting it
- The CAP theorem is examined nearly every year: know what each letter means and why you can only have two

### DTS 314 — Data Management I

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-314
- 3 units · 300 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Database systems for the data professional, going well beyond UUY-DTS 112: advanced SQL, indexing and query performance, transactions and concurrency, and the design of data models that survive real workloads.

**Outline**

1. Review of the relational model and relational algebra
2. Advanced SQL: window functions, common table expressions, recursive queries, set operations
3. Views, stored procedures, triggers and user-defined functions
4. Physical design: storage structures, indexing (B-tree, hash), and when an index hurts
5. Query processing and optimisation; reading an execution plan
6. Transactions: ACID properties, concurrency control, locking, isolation levels and deadlock
7. Recovery, backup strategies and write-ahead logging
8. Database security: privileges, roles, injection prevention and encryption at rest
9. Distributed databases and NoSQL families: key-value, document, column-family and graph stores

**Recommended textbooks**

- Database System Concepts — Silberschatz, Korth & Sudarshan
- SQL Performance Explained — Markus Winand

**How to pass**

- Window functions are the highest-leverage SQL skill you can learn at this level — running totals, rankings and period-over-period comparisons all become one query
- Run EXPLAIN on your slow queries and read the plan. Knowing why a query is slow is a rarer skill than writing SQL at all
- Learn the isolation levels with the anomaly each one permits (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom) — that table is a standing exam question
- Practise on a database with at least a million rows; performance concepts are invisible on toy data

### DTS 318 — Ethics and Legal Issues in Data Science

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-318
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The obligations that come with holding and modelling data about people: privacy law, consent, algorithmic fairness, transparency and accountability. The course that determines whether your technical skill does good or harm.

**Outline**

1. Ethical frameworks applied to data: consequentialist, deontological and virtue perspectives
2. Privacy: informational self-determination, consent, purpose limitation and data minimisation
3. Anonymisation, pseudonymisation and re-identification risk; k-anonymity and differential privacy in outline
4. Data protection law: the Nigeria Data Protection Act, the NDPR, and the GDPR as a comparator
5. Rights of data subjects: access, rectification, erasure, portability and objection
6. Algorithmic bias and fairness: sources of bias, fairness metrics, and their trade-offs
7. Transparency, explainability and the right to an explanation; black-box models in high-stakes decisions
8. Accountability, auditing, and the governance of automated decision-making
9. Professional codes of conduct and case studies of data science failures

**Recommended textbooks**

- Weapons of Math Destruction — Cathy O'Neil
- Ethics and Data Science — Loukides, Mason & Patil
- Fairness and Machine Learning — Barocas, Hardt & Narayanan

**How to pass**

- Know the Nigeria Data Protection Act and the NDPR specifically — Nigerian law is what you are examined on and what will actually govern your work
- Learn why the different fairness metrics are mathematically incompatible; "just make it fair" is not an available option and examiners want you to know that
- Prepare three real case studies (e.g. COMPAS, a credit-scoring case, a facial-recognition case) in enough detail to analyse rather than merely name
- This is the course whose content you will most often actually need after graduation — treat it as professional training, not a compliance box

### GST 311 — Peace and Conflict Resolution

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/gst-311
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: undergraduates across University of Uyo programmes (foundation course, not departmental)

The nature of conflict, the conditions for peace, and the practical machinery of resolution — negotiation, mediation and arbitration. Applied to the Nigerian and West African context.

**Outline**

1. Basic concepts: peace, conflict, violence, security and human security
2. Types and causes of conflict: economic, political, ethnic, religious and resource conflict
3. Theories of conflict and conflict dynamics; conflict escalation and de-escalation
4. Peace as a process: peacekeeping, peacemaking, peacebuilding and peace enforcement
5. Conflict resolution mechanisms: negotiation, mediation, conciliation, arbitration and adjudication
6. Alternative dispute resolution (ADR) and traditional African conflict-resolution systems
7. The role of government, civil society, NGOs and international bodies (UN, AU, ECOWAS)
8. Case studies of conflict and resolution in Nigeria and West Africa
9. Developing a culture of peace; the role of the media and of data in early warning

**Recommended textbooks**

- Peace and Conflict Studies — David P. Barash & Charles P. Webel
- Introduction to Peace and Conflict Resolution — UniUyo GST course team

**How to pass**

- Learn the resolution mechanisms as a ladder from least to most binding (negotiation → mediation → arbitration → adjudication); scenario questions ask you to pick the right rung
- Have two Nigerian case studies fully prepared — specificity is what separates an A from a C in the essay
- Conflict early-warning systems are increasingly data-driven; mentioning that connection is a genuine differentiator in your answers
- This is another GST course of easy marks; do the past questions rather than over-reading

### GST 312 — Peace and Conflict Resolution

### UUY-CYB 314 — Information Security Models

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-cyb-314
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The formal models that underpin access control and multi-level security: Bell-LaPadula, Biba, Clark-Wilson, Brewer-Nash, and the access-control mechanisms (MAC, RBAC, ACLs, lattice-based control) that implement them in real systems.

**Outline**

1. Basic concepts of formal security models; Access Control Lists (ACL)
2. Bell-LaPadula model (confidentiality) and the Biba model (integrity)
3. Brewer and Nash model (Chinese Wall) and the Clark-Wilson model
4. Capability-based security and the Object-Capability Model
5. Context-Based Access Control (CBAC) and Graham-Denning model
6. Harrison-Ruzzo-Ullman (HRU) and the Take-Grant protection model
7. Lattice-Based Access Control (LBAC), Mandatory Access Control (MAC), and Multi-Level Security (MLS)
8. Non-interference security; Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
9. Protection rings and the High-Water Mark security model

**Recommended textbooks**

- Computer Security: Principles and Practice — William Stallings & Lawrie Brown
- Security Engineering — Ross Anderson

**How to pass**

- Contrast Bell-LaPadula (confidentiality: "no read up, no write down") with Biba (integrity: the reverse) — this pairing is exam-critical
- Draw the lattice for MLS/LBAC by hand — visualising the ordering makes the model click
- Link RBAC and MAC back to UUY-CYB 122 and UUY-CYB 221, where these controls are applied practically
- Memorise which model addresses which property (confidentiality, integrity, or conflict of interest) — a common exam table

### UUY-CYB 315 — Lab for Cyber Attacks and Vulnerability Testing

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-cyb-315
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Hands-on laboratory course in offensive/defensive security: operating system file structures, formal security models, intrusion detection, vulnerability testing, and countermeasures for denial-of-service, worm, and virus attacks.

**Outline**

1. Operating system file structure and protection mechanisms
2. Formal models of security
3. Cryptography and steganography
4. Network and distributed system security
5. Vulnerability testing on networked infrastructure
6. Intrusion detection tasks on networked computer systems
7. Denial-of-service attack strategies and prevention
8. Worms and viruses: attack strategies and countermeasures
9. Transfer of funds/value across networks; electronic voting security

**Recommended textbooks**

- The Hacker Playbook 3 — Peter Kim
- Kali Linux Revealed — Raphaël Hertzog & Jim O'Gorman

**How to pass**

- Set up a local lab with VirtualBox + Kali Linux + Metasploitable before the first lab session
- TryHackMe and HackTheBox both have beginner paths that map directly to this lab content — free tiers available
- Document everything in your lab notebook: tools used, commands run, findings, screenshots
- Practise on legal targets ONLY: Metasploitable, DVWA, HackTheBox, TryHackMe — never on live systems
