### UUY-DTS 311 — Analytics of Web Data

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-311
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Measuring and analysing behaviour on the web: clickstream and log data, web analytics platforms, funnels and attribution, plus text and network analysis of web content. Builds directly on UUY-DTS 121.

**Outline**

1. Sources of web data: server logs, clickstream, tags, cookies and event tracking
2. Web analytics platforms: metrics, dimensions, sessions, users and events (GA4 model)
3. Traffic analysis: acquisition channels, bounce and engagement, retention and cohorts
4. Conversion funnels, goals and attribution models
5. Segmentation of web audiences; behavioural clustering
6. A/B testing and experimentation on the web: design, sample size and interpretation
7. Web content mining: scraping at scale, parsing, deduplication and storage
8. Text analytics on web content: tokenisation, TF-IDF, sentiment analysis, topic modelling
9. Web structure mining: link graphs, PageRank, and social network analysis measures

**Recommended textbooks**

- Web Analytics 2.0 — Avinash Kaushik
- Mining the Social Web — Matthew A. Russell & Mikhail Klassen
- Mining of Massive Datasets — Leskovec, Rajaraman & Ullman

**How to pass**

- Set up analytics on any small site (even a personal page) and watch real traffic — the vocabulary only sticks when attached to real numbers
- PageRank is an eigenvector computation, which connects straight back to your linear algebra; understanding it that way is what earns the top marks
- A/B testing is applied DTS 224 — the sample-size and p-value questions are the same statistics in a commercial costume
- Be careful with the ethics of scraping here; the legal boundaries you learned in DTS 318 are examinable in this context too

### UUY-DTS 313 — Machine Learning and Applications

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-313
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The core machine learning course: supervised and unsupervised algorithms, how they are trained, how they are evaluated, and how they fail. The technical centrepiece of the degree.

**Outline**

1. The learning problem: supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised and reinforcement learning
2. Linear and logistic regression; loss functions and gradient descent
3. Regularisation: ridge, lasso, and the bias–variance trade-off revisited
4. k-nearest neighbours, Naive Bayes and support vector machines
5. Decision trees, and ensembles: bagging, random forests and gradient boosting
6. Unsupervised learning: k-means, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN
7. Dimensionality reduction: principal component analysis and t-SNE
8. Model evaluation: confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1, ROC/AUC, cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning
9. Introduction to neural networks: perceptrons, backpropagation, and where deep learning applies

**Recommended textbooks**

- An Introduction to Statistical Learning — James, Witten, Hastie & Tibshirani
- Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras and TensorFlow — Aurélien Géron
- The Elements of Statistical Learning — Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman

**How to pass**

- Accuracy is a misleading metric on imbalanced data — learn precision, recall and the ROC curve properly, and be able to argue which matters for a given problem
- Implement linear regression and k-means from scratch in NumPy once. After that, using scikit-learn is informed rather than magical
- For every algorithm, learn its inductive bias — what it assumes about the data. That is what tells you when to reach for it
- Compete in one beginner Kaggle competition; the feedback loop teaches evaluation discipline faster than any lecture

### UUY-DTS 317 — Basic Operating Systems for Data Science

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-317
- 2 units · 300 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Operating system fundamentals with a practical Linux emphasis: processes, memory, file systems, the shell, and containers. The environment every data pipeline actually runs in.

**Outline**

1. Operating system functions, structure and system calls
2. Processes and threads: states, scheduling, context switching and inter-process communication
3. Concurrency: race conditions, mutual exclusion, semaphores and deadlock
4. Memory management: paging, segmentation, virtual memory and thrashing
5. File systems: structure, permissions, links, mounting and I/O
6. The Linux shell: navigation, pipes and redirection, grep/awk/sed, process control
7. Shell scripting and job scheduling with cron
8. Package management, environments and dependency isolation
9. Virtualisation and containers: Docker images, containers and volumes for reproducible analysis

**Recommended textbooks**

- Operating System Concepts — Silberschatz, Galvin & Gagne
- The Linux Command Line — William Shotts

**How to pass**

- Use Linux (or WSL on Windows) as your daily environment for one semester — nothing else builds shell fluency
- Learn grep, awk, sed and pipes properly: on a 10 GB log file the command line beats pandas, and it beats it by a lot
- Docker is the answer to "it works on my machine" — containerise one of your own projects and the concept lands permanently
- Deadlock conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait) are a guaranteed exam question — memorise all four

### CYB 311 — SIWES I (Student Industrial Work Experience Scheme)

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-311-siwes-1
- 3 units · 300 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The first industrial training placement: three months attached to a private or public organisation during the second-year long break, gaining practical cybersecurity experience under supervision, with a defended report at the end.

**Outline**

1. IT department integration and workplace orientation
2. Practical network administration and monitoring
3. Security operations: log review, alert triage, incident handling
4. Help desk and technical support operations
5. Observing penetration testing or vulnerability management
6. Documenting processes and writing technical reports
7. Professional communication and teamwork in IT environments
8. Identifying and reporting your learning outcomes

**Recommended textbooks**

- SIWES Student Handbook — ITF (Industrial Training Fund)
- The IT Professional's Guide to Career Development — Various

**How to pass**

- Start searching for a placement organisation at the end of 200L second semester — do not wait
- Security operations centres (SOCs), banks, telecoms companies, and NITDA are good placement targets
- Keep a daily log of what you do — your SIWES report grade depends on evidence of engagement
- Ask your supervisor for tasks beyond basic support — every real challenge is a learning opportunity

### CYB 312 — SIWES II (Student Industrial Work Experience Scheme)

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-312-siwes-2
- 3 units · 300 Level · Second Semester

The second, more advanced industrial placement: three months attached to a private or public organisation during the third-year long break, building on SIWES I with additional practical cybersecurity experience and a defended report.

**Outline**

1. Advanced security monitoring and SIEM usage in production
2. Participation in or observation of incident response

4. Security awareness training participation

**Recommended textbooks**

**How to pass**

- Use SIWES to begin working towards a professional certification: Security+, CEH, or OSCP
- Build your LinkedIn profile during SIWES — document your work and achievements professionally
- Network actively: every senior professional you meet is a potential reference or employer
- Your SIWES report is a professional document — write it to the standard you would send to a client

### CYB 313 — Report Writing

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-313-report-writing
- 3 units · 300 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The craft of professional and technical report writing, focused on documenting the SIWES I and II placements: structuring findings, presenting technical work clearly, and defending a written report before a panel.

**Outline**

1. Structure of a professional technical report
2. Documenting workplace experience and technical assignments
3. Clarity, precision, and objectivity in technical writing
4. Figures, tables, and appendices in a technical report
5. Referencing and academic/professional integrity
6. Editing and proofreading technical documents
7. Preparing to defend a written report before a panel
8. Common pitfalls in student technical reports

**Recommended textbooks**

- Technical Report Writing Today — Daniel G. Riordan
- The Elements of Technical Writing — Gary Blake & Robert W. Bly

**How to pass**

- Draft this report alongside your SIWES I/II placements rather than after — memory of details fades fast
- Use the ITF SIWES logbook as your raw source material, then structure it into a formal report
- Have a peer or supervisor read a draft before submission — clarity gaps are hard to see in your own writing
- Practise a short verbal summary of your report; panels often ask you to explain it in your own words

### CYB 314 — Mini Project

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/mini-project-300l

A supervised mini research or development project that demonstrates integration of skills acquired across the first six semesters. Serves as a preparation and rehearsal for the 400L Final Year Project.

1. Topic selection: scope, feasibility, and originality
2. Literature review methodology

8. Oral presentation and project defence

**Recommended textbooks**

- Research Methods for Computer Science — Stuart Shapiro
- Writing for Computer Science — Justin Zobel

**How to pass**

- Choose a project topic that excites you — you will work on it for a full semester
- Select a topic that connects to your SIWES experience — it gives you real-world data and context
- Start your literature review early: academic papers take time to find and read
- The mini project is a rehearsal for FYP — treat it seriously and document everything

### CYB 399 — Seminar

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/seminar-300l
- 3 units · 300 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

A series of student-led presentations on advanced topics in cybersecurity. Develops research, critical analysis, and public speaking skills in a professional academic setting.

**Outline**

1. Selecting a cutting-edge cybersecurity topic
2. Academic literature search and evaluation
3. Structuring a 20-minute technical presentation
4. Slide design for technical audiences
5. Handling questions from examiners and peers
6. Peer review and constructive feedback
7. Current trends: AI security, quantum threat, ransomware economics
8. Writing a seminar paper to accompany the presentation

**Recommended textbooks**

- The Craft of Research — Booth, Colomb & Williams
- Presentation Zen — Garr Reynolds

**How to pass**

- Choose a seminar topic from an area where you have genuine curiosity — passion shows in delivery
- Rehearse your presentation at least three full times before the seminar day
- Anticipate questions: list five things an examiner might ask and prepare short, confident answers
- Clear slides with minimal text and good diagrams outperform bullet-point-heavy decks every time

### DTS 399 — SIWES

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-399
- 6 units · 300 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme — a full-semester supervised industrial placement. Six units and 270 practical hours, the largest single course in the programme, assessed on your logbook, technical report and defence.

**Outline**

1. Securing a placement relevant to data science: analytics teams, banks, telcos, research institutes, government agencies, tech companies
2. Workplace conduct, confidentiality and professional ethics
3. Applying the data lifecycle in an organisational setting
4. Maintaining the SIWES logbook: daily entries, tasks, tools and skills acquired
5. Industrial supervisor and institution-based supervisor assessment
6. Writing the SIWES technical report: structure, evidence and reflection
7. Oral defence of the placement experience
8. Identifying a real-world problem that could become your final-year project

**Recommended textbooks**

- ITF SIWES Guidelines — Industrial Training Fund
- Departmental SIWES Handbook — Department of Data Science, UniUyo

**How to pass**

- Start looking for a placement a full semester early — the good data-related placements go first and generic clerical placements waste your six units
- Fill the logbook the same day, every day. Reconstructing five months of entries the week before submission is obvious to any examiner and costs marks
- Ask to be given at least one end-to-end task you own; a placement where you only observed is very hard to write six units of report about
- Treat SIWES as final-year project reconnaissance — the best projects come from a real problem you saw at your placement

### UUY-DTS 321 — Computing Skills

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-321
- 3 units · 300 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

A wholly practical course consolidating the professional toolchain: version control, environments, testing, documentation and deployment. The skills that make you employable rather than merely knowledgeable.

**Outline**

1. Version control with Git: commits, branches, merging, rebasing, pull requests and collaboration
2. Project structure and dependency management for reproducible analysis
3. Writing clean, documented, reusable code; style guides and code review
4. Testing: unit tests for data code, assertions and data validation
5. Command-line productivity and automation
6. Notebooks vs scripts vs packages: choosing the right artefact
7. Documentation: READMEs, docstrings and technical writing for code
8. Deployment basics: APIs for models, containerisation and cloud hosting
9. Building and presenting a professional portfolio

**Recommended textbooks**

- Pro Git — Scott Chacon & Ben Straub
- The Pragmatic Programmer — David Thomas & Andrew Hunt

**How to pass**

- Make small, frequent commits with real messages. "update" and "final v2 final" are habits that will embarrass you professionally
- Every project you have ever done should end up in a public GitHub repo with a README that explains the problem, the data and the result
- Learn branching and pull requests properly — this is how every team you will ever join actually works
- Testing data code feels unnecessary until a silent schema change corrupts a month of results. Write the assertions

### UUY-DTS 322 — Industry-based Innovation

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-322
- 3 units · 300 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

A practical, industry-facing innovation project: identify a real problem in an organisation or sector, design a data-driven solution, and demonstrate it. Runs alongside SIWES and feeds directly into your final-year work.

**Outline**

1. Identifying an innovation opportunity within an industry context
2. Stakeholder engagement and requirements gathering
3. Design thinking: empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test
4. Assessing data availability, quality and access constraints for a proposed solution
5. Rapid prototyping of a data product
6. Feasibility: technical, operational, economic and legal
7. Measuring impact: defining success metrics before building
8. Pitching a solution to a non-technical audience
9. Documentation and handover of an innovation project

**Recommended textbooks**

- The Lean Startup — Eric Ries
- Data Science for Business — Foster Provost & Tom Fawcett

**How to pass**

- Choose a problem you have personally observed — a real irritation you witnessed at your SIWES placement beats an impressive-sounding invented one
- Check data availability before you commit to an idea; the most common failure here is a great plan with no obtainable data
- Define your success metric in week one and hold yourself to it — this is exactly what UUY-DTS 211 taught you
- Prototype ugly and early. A working rough demo persuades far more than a polished slide deck

### UUY-DTS 323 — Seminar

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-323
- 3 units · 300 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Research and presentation skills: select a current topic in data science, review the literature, and present and defend it before staff and peers. Preparation for the literature review and defence of DTS 417/428.

**Outline**

1. Selecting and scoping a seminar topic in data science
2. Literature search: Google Scholar, arXiv, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, open-access sources
3. Evaluating sources: peer review, preprints, predatory journals and credibility
4. Reading a research paper efficiently: the three-pass method
5. Synthesising a literature review rather than summarising papers one by one
6. Citation and referencing styles; reference managers (Zotero, Mendeley)
7. Academic integrity and plagiarism avoidance
8. Designing effective slides and speaking to a technical audience
9. Handling questions and defending your position

**Recommended textbooks**

- Writing for Computer Science — Justin Zobel
- How to Read a Paper — S. Keshav

**How to pass**

- Pick a topic narrow enough to cover properly — "AI in healthcare" is a book; "deep learning for malaria diagnosis from blood smear images" is a seminar
- Read 15–20 papers but present the synthesis, not the list. A literature review that goes "Paper A said…, Paper B said…" scores poorly
- Use a reference manager from your first paper; reformatting 30 citations by hand is a self-inflicted wound
- Rehearse out loud with a timer at least three times. The questions afterwards are where marks are won and lost — prepare for the obvious ones

## 400 Level

### COS 411 — Research Methodology and Technical Report Writing

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cos-411
- 3 units · 400 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: undergraduates across University of Uyo programmes (foundation course, not departmental)

The rigorous methods for conducting and communicating academic and technical research: research types and approaches, scientific investigation and problem formulation, data collection instruments, and the structure of technical reports. Essential preparation for the Final Year Project.

**Outline**

1. Foundations, types, and approaches of research; significance of research
2. Research methods versus methodology; the research process; criteria for good research
3. Scientific investigation, problem formulation, and definition of the research problem
4. Data collection: primary and secondary data; questionnaires and interview guidelines
5. Research proposals, research plans, and hypothesis formulation and testing
6. Literature review procedure and referencing cited works
7. Sampling design: types and steps in sampling
8. Methods of analysis: processing, interpretation, and presentation of results
9. Types of reports; technical report writing, layout, and documentation standards

**Recommended textbooks**

- Research Methods for Computer Science — Stuart Shapiro
- Writing for Computer Science — Justin Zobel

**How to pass**

- This course is CYB 497 (FYP) preparation — every lecture directly applies to your final year project
- Use Zotero (free reference management software) to organise your literature from the start
- Plagiarism software is used on all final year projects: understand what constitutes academic misconduct
- Begin identifying your FYP topic in this course — approach your supervisor before the semester ends

### CYB 411 — Systems Vulnerability Assessment and Testing

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-411
- 2 units · 400 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Advanced vulnerability assessment methodology: systematic identification, testing, and mitigation of risks to a company's infrastructure. Covers penetration testing methodologies, information gathering, password cracking, social engineering, and reporting at a professional level.

**Outline**

1. Definition of systems vulnerability; assessment and testing methods
2. Mitigation of risks and enhancing infrastructure security
3. Penetration testing methodologies, test planning and scheduling
4. Information gathering and password cracking
5. Social engineering, internal and external penetration testing
6. Router penetration testing, security analysis, reporting and documentation
7. Operating systems fingerprinting and remote network mapping
8. Software and operational vulnerabilities and how to overcome them
9. Attack surface analysis, fuzz testing, patch management, and security auditing

**Recommended textbooks**

- The Hacker Playbook 3 — Peter Kim
- Penetration Testing — Georgia Weidman

**How to pass**

- CVE/CVSS is the universal language of vulnerabilities — understand Base, Temporal, and Environmental scoring
- Practice building a full assessment report from scanner output — this is the deliverable clients pay for
- Connect each discovered vulnerability to the cryptography or network concepts from earlier courses
- OWASP WSTG (Web Security Testing Guide) is the free, comprehensive standard for web assessments

### CYB 412 — Steganography: Access Methods and Data Hiding

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-412
- 2 units · 400 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The art and science of concealing information: history of secret writing, steganography vs encryption, text/image/audio/video steganography techniques, information hiding and steganalysis, and steganography detection.

**Outline**

1. History of secret writing; overview of steganography
2. Why steganography is important; steganography vs encryption
3. Steganography types and methods: text, image, video and audio steganography
4. Survey of steganography techniques for encrypting data
5. Information hiding: steganography and steganalysis
6. Data hiding methods, techniques, and access methods
7. Steganographic algorithms and their security
8. Steganography detection: finding images and verifying hidden content

**Recommended textbooks**

- Hiding in Plain Sight: Steganography and the Art of Covert Communication — Eric Cole
- Digital Steganography and Watermarking — Fátima Terroso-Saenz et al.

**How to pass**

- Implement a simple LSB steganography tool in Python — it takes one hour and permanently fixes the concept
- Understand why steganography matters for forensics: hidden data in images is a real-world challenge
- Tools like Steghide, OpenStego, and SilentEye are free — use them to both hide and detect
- Connect steganography to CYB 423 (Digital Forensics) — detection is a key forensic skill

### CYB 413 — Cyber Threat Intelligence and Cyber Conflict

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-413
- 2 units · 400 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Techniques for detecting, responding to, and defeating organised cybercrime and cyberwar activities. Covers cyber threat intelligence (tactical, operational, and strategic), the kill chain, indicator lifecycle, and the evolution of counterterrorism and cyber conflict.

**Outline**

1. Detecting, responding to, and defeating organised cybercrimes and cyberwar activities
2. Analysing successful and unsuccessful APT and malware campaigns
3. National and international policies for combating cyber terrorism
4. Cyber threat intelligence: defining threats, indicators of compromise
5. Tactical threat intelligence: the kill chain and intrusion analysis; indicator lifecycle
6. Operational threat intelligence: information sharing, campaigns and threat actors
7. Strategic threat intelligence: threat modelling, organisational security posturing
8. Event recording and incident sharing; evolution of counterterrorism and cyber conflict

**Recommended textbooks**

- The Threat Intelligence Handbook — CrowdStrike
- Cyber War: The Next Threat to National Security — Richard A. Clarke & Robert K. Knake

**How to pass**

- MITRE ATT&CK (attack.mitre.org) is free and should be explored thoroughly — it is the industry standard
- Use MISP or OpenCTI in a lab environment to understand how threat intel is operationalised
- APT case studies (APT28/Fancy Bear, APT41, Lazarus Group) provide excellent exam material
- Cyber conflict geopolitics from CYB 211 provides the strategic context — connect them explicitly

### CYB 414 — Cloud Computing Security

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-414
- 2 units · 400 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Securing cloud environments: cloud service and deployment models, data-centre and virtualisation security, the cloud cube model, threat mitigation, and the standards (NIST, Cloud Security Alliance) that govern effective cloud management.

**Outline**

1. Cloud computing, vendors, threats, and the cloud reference model
2. Cloud-enabling technologies, services, and service-oriented architectures
3. Cloud service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) and deployment models (Public, Private, Hybrid, Community)
4. Data centres: servers, storage, networking and virtualisation
5. The cloud cube model and security for cloud computing
6. Cloud threats, threat mitigation, and security risks
7. Cloud Security Alliance, NIST Information Assurance Framework, cloud audit
8. Cloud business continuity planning and architectural best practices for designing for the cloud
9. Economics of the cloud; cloud strategy and standards

**Recommended textbooks**

- Cloud Security and Privacy — Tim Mather, Subra Kumaraswamy & Shahed Latif
- AWS Certified Security Specialty Study Guide — Chad Smith

**How to pass**

- AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud all offer free tiers — create an account and explore IAM hands-on
- Cloud certifications (AWS Security Specialty, Azure SC-900) can be pursued during 400L
- Shared responsibility is the most exam-critical concept: draw the model from memory
- OWASP Cloud Top 10 is a free, authoritative reference for cloud-specific attack vectors

### CYB 497 — Final Year Project I

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-497
- 3 units · 400 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The first phase of the capstone Final Year Project: an independent or group investigation of a cybersecurity-related problem, culminating in a written proposal covering the problem statement, objectives, scope, research gap, and proposed methodology. Supervised closely by an academic supervisor.

**Outline**

1. Identifying a researchable cybersecurity project topic under supervisor guidance
2. Literature review to establish the research gap
3. Referencing and acknowledging sources of information
4. Conceptualising and designing a research methodology
5. Determining tools for analysing data based on research objectives
6. Writing a coherent project proposal: problem, aim, objectives, scope, significance
7. Estimated schedule of completion and resources needed
8. Oral presentation of the written project proposal
9. Emerging-trend topics: AI, steganography, quantum computing, big data, cloud security, ethical hacking, digital forensics, blockchain, IoT, 5G security

**Recommended textbooks**

- Writing for Computer Science — Justin Zobel
- The Craft of Research — Booth, Colomb & Williams

**How to pass**

- Meet your supervisor regularly — at minimum twice a month; consistent updates prevent last-minute crises
- Choose a topic that either solves a real local cybersecurity problem or contributes something novel
- Begin writing from day one: a rough chapter is easier to improve than a blank page
- Document all design decisions and their justifications — examiners ask "why this approach?"

### DTS 413 — Data Visualization for Data-driven Decision Making

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-413
- 2 units · 400 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The theory and craft of visual communication: perception, encoding, chart selection, dashboard design and narrative. How an analysis becomes a decision.

**Outline**

1. Why visualisation works: visual perception, pre-attentive attributes and cognitive load
2. The grammar of graphics: data, aesthetic mappings, geometries, scales, facets
3. Choosing an encoding: position, length, angle, area, colour, shape — and their accuracy ranking
4. Chart selection for comparison, distribution, composition, relationship and trend
5. Colour: sequential, diverging and categorical palettes; colour-blind-safe design
6. Common distortions: truncated axes, dual axes, misleading area, cherry-picked ranges
7. Dashboard design: layout, hierarchy, interactivity and the audience's question
8. Interactive and web visualisation: Plotly, Dash/Streamlit, D3 concepts
9. Data storytelling: narrative structure, annotation and the single message per chart

**Recommended textbooks**

- The Visual Display of Quantitative Information — Edward R. Tufte
- Fundamentals of Data Visualization — Claus O. Wilke
- Storytelling with Data — Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic

**How to pass**

- Learn the accuracy ranking of visual encodings (position beats length beats angle beats area beats colour) — it answers most "which chart?" questions on its own
- Never use a pie chart with more than three slices, and be ready to justify that rule in the exam
- Collect bad charts from newspapers and rebuild them properly; critique-and-redesign is the fastest way to develop judgement
- Every chart should have one message. If you cannot state it in a sentence, split the chart in two

### DTS 417 — Final Year Project I

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-417
- 3 units · 400 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The first half of the capstone: choose a problem, review the literature, design the methodology, secure the data, and defend a proposal. What you do this semester determines whether DTS 428 is manageable or miserable.

**Outline**

1. Selecting a feasible project topic with a genuine data source
2. Defining the problem statement, aims, objectives and research questions
3. Conducting and writing the literature review; establishing the research gap
4. Designing the methodology: data, methods, evaluation criteria and tools
5. Data acquisition, ethical clearance and data-use agreements where required
6. Preliminary exploratory analysis and feasibility demonstration
7. Project planning: milestones, deliverables and risk register
8. Writing chapters one to three of the project report
9. The proposal defence: presenting and defending your design

**Recommended textbooks**

- Research Methodology: Methods and Techniques — C.R. Kothari & Gaurav Garg
- Departmental Project Handbook — Department of Data Science, UniUyo

**How to pass**

- Confirm you can actually obtain the data before you commit to the topic. No-data is the number one cause of a stalled project
- Choose a supervisor whose interests match your topic and agree a fixed meeting rhythm in week one
- Do the entire pipeline on a tiny sample early — an end-to-end rough version in month one beats a perfect chapter one and no code
- Write as you go. Chapters one to three written in the last two weeks are visibly written in the last two weeks

### INS 411 — Project Management

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/ins-411
- 2 units · 400 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: undergraduates across University of Uyo programmes (foundation course, not departmental)

Planning, executing and controlling projects: scope, schedule, cost, risk and stakeholders, across both traditional and agile approaches. Directly applicable to running your final-year project on time.

**Outline**

1. Project characteristics, the project lifecycle and the role of the project manager
2. Project initiation: charter, stakeholders and scope definition
3. Work breakdown structure and activity definition
4. Scheduling: Gantt charts, network diagrams, CPM and PERT; critical path and float
5. Resource allocation, levelling and cost estimation; budgeting
6. Risk management: identification, qualitative and quantitative analysis, response planning
7. Quality management and change control
8. Agile approaches: Scrum roles, sprints, backlogs and ceremonies; Kanban
9. Monitoring and control: earned value analysis; project closure and lessons learned

**Recommended textbooks**

- A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide) — Project Management Institute
- Project Management: A Systems Approach — Harold Kerzner

**How to pass**

- CPM/PERT network problems are guaranteed and are pure method marks — practise drawing the network, computing earliest/latest times and identifying the critical path until it is mechanical
- Know the difference between agile and waterfall well enough to argue which suits a data science project (usually agile — requirements shift as you learn what the data supports)
- Actually build a Gantt chart for your DTS 417 project; students who plan their project finish it
- Learn the earned value formulas (CV, SV, CPI, SPI) — they are compact, examinable and frequently forgotten

### UUY-CYB 411 — Business Intelligence in Small and Medium-Scale Enterprises (BISME)

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-cyb-411
- 2 units · 400 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Data analytics and business intelligence tools in the context of small and medium enterprises: BI applications in Excel and R, reporting tools, data warehousing and dimensional modelling, ETL, and how BI connects to big data and cloud computing.

**Outline**

1. Overview of BI concepts and applications using Excel and R
2. SQL Server Reporting Services, Power BI, and Tableau
3. BI architecture: data warehouse and BI architecture framework
4. BI development approaches: Kimball's bus architecture vs Inmon's Corporate Information Factory
5. Data governance and the TDWI BI maturity model
6. Data models: entity-relationship (E/R) and dimensional modelling; OLAP
7. Data integration: extract, transform, load (ETL)
8. Big data and cloud computing in relation to BI and business analytics

**Recommended textbooks**

- Business Intelligence: A Managerial Perspective on Analytics — Ramesh Sharda, Dursun Delen & Efraim Turban
- Data Warehousing in the Age of Big Data — Krish Krishnan

**How to pass**

- Microsoft Power BI Desktop is free — build a real dashboard using any Nigerian public dataset
- Star schema vs snowflake schema is exam-critical — understand the trade-offs with real examples
- Connect BI security to CYB 224 (Data Security) — BI platforms are high-value data targets
- Microsoft Learn (free) has a complete Power BI learning path with certifications

### UUY-DTS 410 — Special Topics in Data Science

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-410
- 2 units · 400 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

A rotating course on current developments in the field — the content varies year to year with staff expertise and what is moving in the discipline. Recent themes include deep learning, large language models, MLOps and causal inference.

**Outline**

1. Current research directions in data science and machine learning
2. Deep learning architectures: CNNs for images, RNNs/Transformers for sequences
3. Large language models: pretraining, fine-tuning, prompting and retrieval-augmented generation
4. Natural language processing pipelines and embeddings
5. MLOps: experiment tracking, model registries, monitoring and drift detection
6. Causal inference: correlation vs causation, randomised experiments, difference-in-differences
7. Responsible and explainable AI: SHAP, LIME and model interpretability
8. Edge cases and emerging areas: federated learning, synthetic data, AutoML
9. Reading and critiquing a current research paper

**Recommended textbooks**

- Deep Learning — Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville
- Designing Machine Learning Systems — Chip Huyen

**How to pass**

- Confirm this year's actual syllabus with the lecturer in week one — the content genuinely rotates, so last year's notes may not apply
- Whatever the theme, the assessment usually involves reading current papers; practise the three-pass method from UUY-DTS 323
- This is the course closest to what employers are hiring for right now — treat it as career investment, not a filler 2 units
- Reproduce one result from a paper on a small dataset; "I reimplemented it" is a strong thing to say in an interview

### UUY-DTS 411 — Bio-Analytics Systems and Applications

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-411
- 2 units · 400 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Data science applied to biological and health data: genomics, clinical records, epidemiological modelling and public-health surveillance, with the specific statistical and ethical challenges those domains bring.

**Outline**

1. Introduction to biological data: genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic and clinical data types
2. Biological databases and formats: GenBank, FASTA/FASTQ, VCF, UniProt
3. Sequence analysis: alignment, BLAST, and motif finding
4. Gene expression analysis and the high-dimension/low-sample-size problem
5. Multiple testing and false discovery rate correction
6. Electronic health records: structure, coding systems (ICD, SNOMED) and data quality
7. Survival analysis: Kaplan–Meier curves, hazard functions, Cox regression
8. Epidemiological modelling: incidence, prevalence, SIR/SEIR compartment models
9. Health data privacy, consent and the ethics of biomedical data

**Recommended textbooks**

- Bioinformatics and Functional Genomics — Jonathan Pevsner
- Biostatistics: A Foundation for Analysis in the Health Sciences — Daniel & Cross

**How to pass**

- The multiple-testing problem is the defining statistical issue in genomics: with 20,000 genes tested at p < 0.05 you get 1,000 false positives by chance. Understand Bonferroni and Benjamini–Hochberg
- Survival analysis is the one technique here that transfers everywhere — customer churn and equipment failure are the same mathematics
- Use real public data (NCBI, WHO, NCDC) for practicals; health data science is unusually well served by open datasets
- The ethics content is not decorative — health data carries the strictest consent and privacy obligations of any domain you will work in

### UUY-DTS 412 — Data Management II

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-412
- 2 units · 400 Level · First Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Enterprise-scale data management, continuing DTS 314: data architecture, pipelines and orchestration, master data and quality management, governance, and the modern data stack.

**Outline**

1. Enterprise data architecture: operational vs analytical systems
2. Data integration: ETL vs ELT, batch vs streaming ingestion
3. Pipeline orchestration and scheduling; DAGs and tools such as Airflow
4. Data lakes, data warehouses and the lakehouse pattern; file formats (Parquet, Avro, ORC)
5. Master data management and reference data
6. Data quality: dimensions, profiling, validation rules and monitoring
7. Metadata management, data catalogues and data lineage
8. Data governance: ownership, stewardship, policy and regulatory compliance
9. Data lifecycle management: retention, archiving and secure disposal

**Recommended textbooks**

- Fundamentals of Data Engineering — Joe Reis & Matt Housley
- DAMA-DMBOK: Data Management Body of Knowledge — DAMA International
- The Data Warehouse Toolkit — Ralph Kimball & Margy Ross

**How to pass**

- Build one real pipeline end to end (ingest → transform → store → schedule), even a small one. Data engineering is understood by doing
- Know why Parquet beats CSV for analytics (columnar, compressed, typed) — a favourite short-answer question and a genuinely useful fact
- Data quality dimensions (accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness) are examinable as a list — memorise them
- Governance sounds bureaucratic until you inherit an undocumented database. Frame your answers around that reality

### CYB 421 — Ethical Hacking and Reverse Engineering

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-421
- 2 units · 400 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Advanced offensive security: perimeter defences, privilege escalation, malware and social engineering, system and network hacking, web/wireless/mobile attacks, and reverse engineering of code and network exploits as a method for developing countermeasures.

**Outline**

1. Ethical hacking strategies; how perimeter defences work and how intruders escalate privileges
2. Intrusion detection, policy creation, and social engineering
3. Attack phases; footprinting, reconnaissance, and scanning networks
4. Enumeration, system hacking, and malware threats; sniffing; physical security
5. Password vulnerabilities and cracking passwords
6. Denial of service, session hijacking; hacking web servers and web applications, SQL injection
7. Hacking wireless networks and mobile platforms
8. Evading IDS, firewalls, and honeypots
9. Reverse engineering of code and network exploits for countermeasure development

**Recommended textbooks**

- Hacking: The Art of Exploitation — Jon Erickson
- Practical Malware Analysis — Sikorski & Honig

**How to pass**

- Ghidra (from the NSA — free) is the primary tool for this course: practise weekly from 300L onward
- Buffer overflows become clearer once you understand assembly and memory layout — invest the time
- Malware.analysis.me and ANY.RUN provide safe malware samples and sandboxes for practice
- OSCP certification aligns almost perfectly with this course — consider it post-graduation

### CYB 422 — Deep and Dark Web Security

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-422
- 2 units · 400 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The architecture, technologies, and security landscape of the dark web. Covers Tor network internals, cryptocurrency and crypto-trading, safe and anonymous access techniques, and the risks and monitoring of dark/deep web activity.

**Outline**

1. Dark web, deep web, and clear net; how to get on the dark web
2. Tor, onion routing, hidden services, and Tor alternatives (I2P, Matrix, Orbot, FreeNet)
3. Privacy and anonymity; accessing the deep/dark web via VPN + Tor safely
4. Cryptocurrencies: crypto trading, cryptomining, anonymity and security
5. Navigating the dark web: search engines, the Hidden Wiki, darknet email and messaging
6. Dark web markets and takedown case studies (Silk Road and others)
7. Cyber threats and dangers on the deep/dark web; safety practices
8. Dark web and deep web monitoring

**Recommended textbooks**

- Dark Web Intelligence — Joseph M. Straw
- Tor and the Dark Art of Anonymity — Lance Henderson

**How to pass**

- Use Tor Browser (legal) to understand the surface experience — but only on trusted, legal .onion sites
- Dark web case studies (Silk Road, BTC-e, AlphaBay takedowns) are the best exam material
- Distinguish carefully between anonymity and privacy — examiners look for precision
- OSINT Forum and Intel Techniques (Michael Bazzell) provide excellent, legal dark web investigation training

### CYB 423 — Digital Forensics and Investigation Methods

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-423
- 2 units · 400 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The science and practice of digital forensics: securing, processing, acquiring, examining, and reporting digital evidence; the cyber trail; and the role of computers in crime, technology, and law. Covers portable and stationary device forensics.

**Outline**

1. Introduction to digital forensics and digital evidence
2. Challenging aspects of digital evidence; best practices in securing and processing evidence
3. The cyber trail and its challenges; cyber auditing
4. Brief history of computer crime and cybercrime investigation; evolution of investigative tools
5. Role of computers in crime, technology, and law: jurisdiction, privacy, copyright, digital IP theft
6. The investigative process and investigative reconstruction with digital evidence
7. Techniques and tools for computer forensics: acquisition, preservation, recovery, analysis
8. Forensic examination of portable and stationary storage devices, PDAs, and cell phones

**Recommended textbooks**

- Digital Forensics with Open Source Tools — Cory Altheide & Harlan Carvey
- The Art of Memory Forensics — Ligh, Case, Levy & Walters

**How to pass**

- Autopsy (free, open source) is the standard forensic tool for this course — install and practise immediately
- DFIR.training has free forensic exercises and challenge images — the best way to build skill
- Chain of custody documentation is as important as technical analysis in real cases — know it perfectly
- Connect steganography detection (CYB 412) and network analysis (UUY-CYB 221) to forensics workflows

### CYB 498 — Final Year Project II

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/cyb-498
- 3 units · 400 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

A continuation of CYB 497: completing the research methodology, statistical data analysis, prototype/simulation development, and the formal written report (chapters four and five), submitted for final grading with an oral defence before the external examiner.

**Outline**

1. Continuation of CYB 497: research methodology and data analysis using statistical tools
2. Performance evaluation of the research/development work
3. Standard documentation of the project and referencing style
4. Programming of the prototype or simulation model, where required
5. Plagiarism and grammar checks
6. Chapters four and five of the formal written report, approved by the supervisor
7. PowerPoint presentation skills
8. Oral defence of the project in the final examination before the external examiner

**Recommended textbooks**

- Writing for Computer Science — Justin Zobel
- How to Write a Better Thesis — Evans, Gruba & Zobel

**How to pass**

- Do not submit on the deadline — submit at least 48 hours early; technical problems are common
- Have at least two people proofread your thesis before submission
- For the viva, prepare a 10-minute verbal summary of your project and its contribution
- Know your own work deeply enough to answer "why did you not use X approach?" for every major decision

### DTS 426 — Data Science Innovation and Entrepreneurship

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-426
- 2 units · 400 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Entrepreneurship specific to data: what makes a data product commercially viable, how data businesses are structured, and how to price, protect and scale an offering built on data and models.

**Outline**

1. The data product landscape: analytics services, embedded models, data marketplaces, decision tools
2. Identifying commercially viable data opportunities; the value of a prediction
3. Data as an asset: acquisition, ownership, licensing and the data moat
4. Business models for data products: subscription, usage-based, freemium, marketplace
5. Costing a data product: infrastructure, compute, storage and human-in-the-loop costs
6. Building an MVP for a data product; when a spreadsheet is the right first version
7. Intellectual property for data and models; trade secrets vs patents
8. Regulatory constraints on data businesses in Nigeria
9. Scaling: from a one-off analysis to a repeatable, automated service

**Recommended textbooks**

- Data Science for Business — Foster Provost & Tom Fawcett
- Prediction Machines — Agrawal, Gans & Goldfarb

**How to pass**

- The central question of this course is "who pays, and why?" — a technically excellent model with no buyer is a hobby
- Prediction Machines' framing (AI reduces the cost of prediction; judgement becomes the scarce input) is a genuinely useful lens for essay answers
- Cost out the infrastructure for your idea honestly; cloud compute has bankrupted more data startups than bad models have
- Combine this with ENT 321 and DTS 428 — one coherent venture built on your project is worth far more than three disconnected submissions

### DTS 428 — Final Year Project II

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/dts-428
- 3 units · 400 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

The capstone completed: implement the methodology designed in DTS 417, evaluate the results, write the full report and defend it. The single largest determinant of your final-year classification.

**Outline**

1. Implementing the methodology: data preparation, modelling and iteration
2. Experimental rigour: baselines, controls, reproducible pipelines and version control
3. Evaluation against the criteria set in the proposal; statistical validity of the comparison
4. Interpreting results honestly, including negative and inconclusive findings
5. Writing chapters four and five: results, discussion, conclusion and recommendations
6. Producing publication-quality tables and figures
7. Assembling the complete report to the departmental format
8. Preparing the demonstration/artefact for assessment
9. The final defence: presentation, demonstration and viva questions

**Recommended textbooks**

- Writing for Computer Science — Justin Zobel
- Departmental Project Handbook — Department of Data Science, UniUyo

**How to pass**

- A negative result honestly analysed scores better than a suspiciously perfect one. Examiners have seen fabricated accuracy figures before
- Always report a baseline. "My model got 87%" means nothing without "and the trivial baseline gets 85%"
- Rehearse the defence with a friend playing hostile examiner. Prepare specifically for "why this method and not X?" and "what are the limitations?"
- Freeze your code and results two weeks before submission and spend that time on the report. Late changes are what break projects

### ENT 321 — Venture Creation

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/ent-321
- 2 units · 400 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: undergraduates across University of Uyo programmes (foundation course, not departmental)

The practical mechanics of launching a business: opportunity identification, business planning, entrepreneurial finance, marketing and e-commerce, and applying emerging technologies to new ventures. Prepares graduates who want to start consultancies or technology ventures.

**Outline**

1. Opportunity identification: sources of business opportunities in Nigeria, market gaps
2. New business development: business planning and market research
3. Entrepreneurial finance: venture capital, microfinance, business plan competitions
4. Entrepreneurial marketing and e-commerce: B2B, B2C, C2C models
5. Small business/family business management: leadership, basic bookkeeping
6. Negotiation and business communication
7. Opportunity discovery: idea generation, pitching, brainstorming
8. Technological solutions for new ventures: AI, VR/MR, IoT, Blockchain, Cloud Computing

**Recommended textbooks**

- Entrepreneurship: Successfully Launching New Ventures — Barringer & Ireland
- Zero to One — Peter Thiel & Blake Masters

**How to pass**

- Actually complete the CAC registration process research — knowing the real steps sets exam answers apart
- Frame your venture creation around a real service gap you identified during SIWES
- A completed business plan is typically the coursework submission — start it week one
- Connect this to ENT 221 — build on the feasibility study you conceptualised in 200L

### UNIUYO-CYB 425 — VoIP and Multimedia Security

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uniuyo-cyb-425-voip
- 2 units · 400 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Securing voice-over-IP and multimedia traffic: VoIP network architecture and call-control protocols (H.323, SIP, MGCP), NAT/firewall traversal, and the encryption and best practices that mitigate VoIP-specific risks.

**Outline**

1. Multimedia elements, characteristics, and storage formats
2. Techniques for streaming data traffic: VoIP and multimedia traffic
3. VoIP network architecture and protocols; SIP-based VoIP security issues
4. Call-control protocols: H.323, Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), MGCP — threats and security holes
5. How NAT and firewalls impact call setup, media streams, and latency
6. SIP NAT traversal: STUN, TURN, and ICE
7. VoIP risks, threats, vulnerabilities, and cryptographic protocols for VoIP security
8. VoIP management tools and best practices for risk mitigation

**Recommended textbooks**

- VoIP and PBX Security and Forensics — Iosif I. Androulidakis
- Hacking VoIP — Himanshu Dwivedi

**How to pass**

- Draw the SIP call-setup flow from memory — most exam questions probe understanding of the signalling sequence
- Understand why NAT breaks VoIP by default before learning STUN/TURN/ICE as the fix — the problem motivates the solution
- Connect VoIP encryption (SRTP, TLS for SIP) back to the cryptography course (CYB 311)
- Wireshark can capture and analyse real SIP/RTP traffic in a lab — practise identifying a call setup in a capture

### UUY-CYB 424 — Enterprise Security and Information Assurance

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-cyb-424
- 2 units · 400 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Security governance at the enterprise level: information security principles, governance and risk management, security architecture and design, and end-to-end security of e-business and cyber environments — from data-centre security to backup and disaster recovery.

**Outline**

1. Information security principles; governance and risk management
2. Security architecture and design
3. Security of e-business and cyber environments end-to-end, including data-centre and access security
4. The information security phases: inspection, protection, detection, reaction, reflection
5. Server and application security; virtual local area networks (VLANs)
6. Secure access and financial transaction techniques
7. Backup and disaster recovery techniques
8. Software development security; law, investigations, and ethics

**Recommended textbooks**

- Official (ISC)² Guide to the CISSP CBK — Adam Gordon
- Information Security Management Handbook — Harold F. Tipton & Kevin Henry

**How to pass**

- ISO 27001 is the global standard for information security management — understand Annex A controls
- The five information security phases (inspection, protection, detection, reaction, reflection) are exam-critical — memorise the sequence
- The CISSP certification is the gold standard for enterprise security leadership — this course is a foundation
- Security policy writing is a practical exam task: practise writing an acceptable use policy from scratch

### UUY-DTS 421 — Data Science Risk and Management

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-421
- 2 units · 400 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

What goes wrong with data and models, and how to manage it: model risk, data risk, operational failure, and the governance structures that catch problems before they reach production.

**Outline**

1. Risk concepts: threat, vulnerability, likelihood, impact and the risk register
2. Data risk: quality failures, silent schema change, leakage, and loss of provenance
3. Model risk: overfitting, target leakage, spurious correlation, and inappropriate deployment
4. Concept drift and data drift; monitoring models in production
5. Bias, fairness and discrimination risk in deployed models
6. Security risk for data systems: access control, adversarial inputs, model theft, privacy attacks
7. Regulatory and compliance risk; auditability of automated decisions
8. Model risk management frameworks, validation and independent review
9. Business continuity, incident response and post-incident review for data systems

**Recommended textbooks**

- Designing Machine Learning Systems — Chip Huyen
- Weapons of Math Destruction — Cathy O'Neil
- ISO 31000 / NIST AI Risk Management Framework — ISO / NIST

**How to pass**

- Target leakage is the classic silent killer: a feature that would not exist at prediction time gives 99% accuracy in testing and fails completely in production. Learn to spot it
- Be able to distinguish data drift (the inputs changed) from concept drift (the relationship changed) with an example of each
- Build a risk register for your DTS 428 project — it is real practice and it genuinely protects the project
- The NIST AI RMF is free, short and current; reading it is the highest-value hour you can spend on this course

### UUY-DTS 422 — Cloud Application Development

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-422
- 2 units · 400 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Building and deploying applications on cloud infrastructure: service models, core compute and storage services, containers and serverless, and the deployment of data and ML workloads to the cloud.

**Outline**

1. Cloud computing concepts: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS; public, private and hybrid clouds
2. Core cloud services: virtual machines, object storage, managed databases, networking basics
3. Identity and access management; the principle of least privilege
4. Containers in the cloud: images, registries and orchestration concepts
5. Serverless computing: functions, event-driven architecture and their trade-offs
6. Building and deploying a REST API for a model
7. Managed data and ML services on cloud platforms
8. Infrastructure as code and CI/CD pipelines
9. Cost management, scaling, monitoring and cloud security fundamentals

**Recommended textbooks**

- Cloud Computing: Concepts, Technology and Architecture — Thomas Erl
- Architecting the Cloud — Michael J. Kavis

**How to pass**

- Use a free tier (AWS, GCP or Azure) and deploy something real. Set a billing alert first — every student has a horror story
- Deploy your DTS 428 model as an API; a live URL in your project defence is memorable and demonstrates the whole stack
- IaaS/PaaS/SaaS classification questions are guaranteed — have a concrete example of each ready
- Least privilege is the security rule that matters most here, and the one most often violated in student projects

### UUY-DTS 423 — Data Warehousing and Multidimensional Modeling

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-423
- 2 units · 400 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Designing the analytical database: dimensional modelling, star and snowflake schemas, slowly changing dimensions, OLAP operations, and the ETL that populates it all.

**Outline**

1. Why analytical and operational databases differ: OLTP vs OLAP workloads
2. Data warehouse architecture: staging, core warehouse, data marts; Inmon vs Kimball approaches
3. Dimensional modelling: facts, dimensions, grain, and the four-step design process
4. Star schema and snowflake schema; when to denormalise
5. Fact table types: transaction, periodic snapshot and accumulating snapshot
6. Dimension design: surrogate keys, hierarchies, conformed dimensions, degenerate dimensions
7. Slowly changing dimensions: Types 0 through 3 and their trade-offs
8. OLAP operations: roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice and pivot; cubes and MOLAP/ROLAP
9. ETL design for the warehouse; incremental loading and change data capture

**Recommended textbooks**

- The Data Warehouse Toolkit — Ralph Kimball & Margy Ross
- Building the Data Warehouse — W.H. Inmon

**How to pass**

- Kimball's four-step process (choose the business process, declare the grain, identify dimensions, identify facts) is the exam's favourite structured answer — memorise it and apply it to any scenario given
- Declaring the grain is the step students skip and the step everything depends on. State it as a single sentence: "one row per…"
- SCD Type 2 (add a new row with validity dates) is the most examined and the most used in practice — be able to draw the before/after table
- Design a small warehouse for a scenario you know (university results, a shop's sales) — it makes every abstract term concrete

### UUY-DTS 424 — Intelligent Computing and Analytics for Urban Centres

- URL: https://www.aretecyb.tech/courses/uuy-dts-424
- 2 units · 400 Level · Second Semester
- Taken by: the departments whose catalogue lists it

Data science applied to cities: sensor and IoT data, mobility and transport analytics, geospatial analysis, and the smart-city systems that use them — with the Nigerian urban context front and centre.

**Outline**

1. Smart city concepts, domains and architectures
2. Urban data sources: IoT sensors, GPS traces, mobile network data, satellite imagery, open city data
3. IoT fundamentals for urban sensing: devices, gateways, protocols (MQTT, LoRaWAN) and edge computing
4. Geospatial data: coordinate systems, vector and raster data, GeoJSON and shapefiles
5. Spatial analysis: geocoding, spatial joins, buffers, density and hotspot analysis
6. Mobility and transport analytics: origin–destination matrices, traffic flow, route optimisation
7. Urban applications: energy, waste, water, public safety, health and environmental monitoring
8. Real-time dashboards and decision support for city administration
9. Challenges in the Nigerian context: data scarcity, informal settlements, infrastructure and surveillance ethics

**Recommended textbooks**

- Urban Analytics — Alex Singleton, Seth Spielman & David Folch
- Geographic Data Science with Python — Rey, Arribas-Bel & Wolf

**How to pass**

- Learn GeoPandas and QGIS practically — geospatial skills are rare among Nigerian graduates and immediately marketable
- Coordinate reference systems cause more bugs than any other geospatial topic; understand why you cannot mix WGS84 and a projected CRS in one calculation
- Use real local data (OpenStreetMap for Uyo, NASA/Copernicus satellite imagery) — a local case study is far stronger in assessment than a foreign one
- The surveillance-ethics angle connects straight back to DTS 318; smart-city sensing is one of the sharpest privacy trade-offs in the field
